query:
Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. How commercially viable is sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization?
1. Who has commercialized it (printer vendors, feedstock suppliers, parts services), with founding
   dates, funding, ownership changes and failures (for example Holo's 2024 asset sale to Greene Group,
   and Nano Dimension's 2022 purchase and 2025 exit of Admatec), and installed base where reported.
2. Which markets and applications have actually adopted it, with named examples: orthodontic and
   dental parts, medical and surgical instruments, watch and jewelry parts, micromechanics, RF and
   microwave parts, copper cold plates and heat sinks for electronics, electrical interconnects,
   nozzles and fluidics, tooling inserts, and any defense or aerospace use.
3. Economics: printer price, feedstock cost, build rate, parts per build, cost per part against MIM
   (break-even volume once mold tooling is counted), binder jetting and micro laser powder bed fusion,
   and typical lead times.
4. Barriers: part size and wall-thickness limits, feedstock availability, qualification and standards
   (MPIF Standard 35, ISO/ASTM 52900 classification), the key patents and who holds them, and
   competition.
5. Your judgement of where the process is headed and which niches it can hold.
Cite peer-reviewed papers, standards, market reports and trade press, and flag any figure that comes
only from a vendor.
task_summary: Assess Commercial Viability Of Sinter-Based Metal Vat Photopolymerization Across Commercialization Markets Economics Barriers And Outlook

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation
        - NON_RANDOMIZED: Non-randomized allocation
        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment
        - PARALLEL: Parallel assignment
        - CROSSOVER: Crossover assignment
        - FACTORIAL: Factorial assignment
        - SEQUENTIAL: Sequential assignment

    ObservationalModel:
        - COHORT: Cohort
        - CASE_CONTROL: Case-Control
        - CASE_ONLY: Case-Only
        - CASE_CROSSOVER: Case-Crossover
        - ECOLOGIC_OR_COMMUNITY: Ecologic or Community
        - FAMILY_BASED: Family-Based
        - DEFINED_POPULATION: Defined Population
        - NATURAL_HISTORY: Natural History
        - OTHER: Other

    DesignMasking:
        - NONE: None (Open Label)
        - SINGLE: Single
        - DOUBLE: Double
        - TRIPLE: Triple
        - QUADRUPLE: Quadruple

    WhoMasked:
        - PARTICIPANT: Participant
        - CARE_PROVIDER: Care Provider
        - INVESTIGATOR: Investigator
        - OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR: Outcomes Assessor

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and

Abstract:
Conversion of inorganic-organic frameworks (ceramic precursors and ceramic-polymer mixtures) into solid mass ceramic structures based on photopolymerization process is currently receiving plentiful attention in the field of additive manufacturing (3D printing). Various techniques (e.g., stereolithography, digital light processing, and two-photon polymerization) that are compatible with this strategy have so far been widely investigated. This is due to their cost-viability, flexibility, and ability to design and manufacture complex geometric structures. Different platforms related to these techniques have been developed too, in order to meet up with modern technology demand. Most relevant to this review are the challenges faced by the researchers in using these 3D printing techniques for the fabrication of ceramic structures. These challenges often range from shape shrinkage, mass loss, poor densification, cracking, weak mechanical performance to undesirable surface roughness of the final ceramic structures. This is due to the brittle nature of ceramic materials. Based on the summary and discussion on the current progress of material-technique correlation available, here we show the significance of material composition and printing processes in addressing these challenges. The use of appropriate solid loading, solvent, and preceramic polymers in forming slurries is suggested as steps in the right direction. Techniques are indicated as another factor playing vital roles and their selection and development are suggested as plausible ways to remove these barriers.

Abstract:
Lithography-based additive manufacturing methods emerged as a powerful method for manufacturing of complex-shaped ceramic parts with excellent functional and structural properties. This paper summarizes the current state of the art in this field by articulating technological challenges associated with printing of functional parts. In addition, the paper addresses process requirements towards further enhancing component quality. A key aspect for obtaining high-quality parts is related to controlling chemical composition and uniformity of the photopolymerizable slurries. The latter requires in-depth understanding of the underlying photochemical processes. Changes in the formulation of the resin as well as changes in the exposure strategy distinctly influence bond conversion and gelling, which, in turn, influence the properties of the green part during thermal processing. Properly optimized processes and material composition allow to target a variety of challenging applications including patient specific parts for digital dentistry, and 3D-printed ceramics which can operate in harsh environments, as may be required in aerospace or chemical engineering applications. The paper will also provide an outlook into novel opportunities for 3D-printed ceramics.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) can revolutionise engineering by taking advantage of unconstrained design and overcoming the limitations of traditional manufacturing capabilities. A promising application of AM is in catalyst substrate manufacturing, aimed at the enhancement of the catalytic efficiency and reduction in the volume and weight of the catalytic reactors in the exhaust gas aftertreatment systems. This work addresses the design and fabrication of innovative, hybrid monolithic ceramic substrates using AM technology based on Digital Light Processing (DLP). The designs are based on two individual substrates integrated into a single, dual-substrate monolith by various interlocking systems. These novel dual-substrate monoliths lay the foundation for the potential reduction in the complexity and expense of the aftertreatment system. Several examples of interlocking systems for dual substrates were designed, manufactured and thermally post-processed to illustrate the viability and versatility of the DLP manufacturing process. Based on the findings, the sintered parts displayed anisotropic sintering shrinkage of approximately 14% in the X–Y direction and 19% in the Z direction, with a sintered density of 97.88 ± 0.01%. Finally, mechanical tests revealed the mechanical integrity of the designed interlocks. U-lock and Thread configurations were found to sustain more load until complete failure.

## 1. segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2 (Context ID: pqac-00000000)

Lithography-Based Metal Manufacturing: Metal-Filled Photoresins,
Cure–Loading Trade-Offs, Debinding, Sintering and Qualification
Optical–Rheological Coupling, Green-State Evidence and Complete-Cell Control

3Dresyns by Resyner Technologies S.L.
Juan Segurola
Correspondence: [email redacted] · Website: www.3Dresyns.com
Engineering Review · ER-149 · Version 0.2 · 5 September 2026

Statement of Significance
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing can shape fine metal-rich features by patterned photopolymerisation without melting metal in
the printer. The apparent precision of projected light does not remove the material difficulty: metal powder must remain dispersed in a
binder that can be coated or renewed, transmit or redistribute enough light to create a controlled green layer, release from the exposure
interface, survive recovery and cleaning, open safe transport paths during binder removal and densify without unacceptable chemistry
change or distortion. Powder loading, viscosity, yield stress, thixotropy, sedimentation, absorption, scattering, cure depth, lateral overcure
and green strength are not independent controls. Nor is a support-free green print necessarily support-free in the furnace. This review
defines the route as a complete indirect chain from released powder, binder and optical system to an accepted metal component. It
separates green photopolymer conversion from debinding and metallurgical densification, bounds published high-resolution and material
demonstrations to their tested systems, and replaces printer-centred claims with part-linked factory evidence.

Abstract
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing uses patterned light to solidify a photoactive metal-powder/binder system layer by layer,
producing a green composite that is subsequently cleaned, debound and sintered or otherwise densified. Literature labels such as LMM,
LMAM, metal DLP, micro-DLP and metal stereolithography cover related but not necessarily identical material-delivery and exposure
architectures. Liquid suspensions, thixotropic pastes and temperature-conditioned feedstocks impose different mixing, sedimentation,
recoating, separation and recovery burdens. Increasing metal loading can reduce organic content and support final densification, while
increasing viscosity, reducing layer renewal and changing optical attenuation and scattering. A nominal wavelength, pixel pitch or scalar
dose cannot predict cured geometry without the spectrum, irradiance map, powder/resin optical state, initiator response, exposure
sequence and measurement method. The exposed object remains a green metal–polymer composite; cure depth, green strength and
apparent feature fidelity do not establish final metal. Binder removal  is governed by chemistry, transport length, gas evolution,
atmosphere and evolving pore pathways. Sintering changes dimensions, pores, chemistry and microstructure under gravity and setter
interaction, so shrinkage cannot be qualified by one scale factor. This qualitative engineering review maps material preparation, light
delivery, green recovery, debinding, densification, factory economics, safety, inspection and qualification. It provides no transferable
formulation, exposure, cleaning, furnace, compensation or acceptance recipe.
Keywords: lithography-based metal manufacturing; metal DLP; vat photopolymerisation; metal-filled photoresin; cure depth; green part;
debinding; sintering; shrinkage; qualification

1. Purpose and scope
  ISO/ASTM 52900 defines vat photopolymerisation as an additive-manufacturing category in which liquid photopolymer in a vat is
selectively cured by light-activated polymerisation [1]. ER-149 addresses the indirect metal subset in which patterned exposure retains
metal powder inside a photoreactive organic phase. The printer creates a green composite, not molten, bonded or service-ready metal. The
delivered metal state exists only after declared recovery and cleaning, binder removal, sintering or another densification operation,
cooling, finishing and inspection.
   The scope includes metal-powder and binder receipt, photoinitiator/absorber/dispersant and additive control, mixing, deagglomeration,
degassing, storage, sampling, temperature conditioning, suspension or paste renewal, layer coating or recoating, optical exposure,
separation or platform movement, green release, unexposed-feedstock removal, cleaning, support or raft removal, green storage and
inspection,  solvent/water/catalytic/thermal  binder  removal  where  specified,  brown-state  control,  sintering,  setters,  dimensional
compensation, optional HIP or heat treatment, machining, surface treatment, cleaning, inspection, production economics, safety and
qualification.
   The terms `lithography-based metal manufacturing`, `lithography metal additive manufacturing`, `metal DLP`, `micro-DLP` and
`stereolithography of metals` are used only with the implementation described by the cited source. They do not establish an identical vat,
film, paste-delivery, recoating, exposure or separation mechanism. NIST treats VPP as an architecture requiring light and material
metrology rather than a generic exposure-time setting [13]. The 2026 NIST photopolymer workshop report likewise identifies unresolved
measurement, data, safety and standards gaps across photopolymer AM [14].
   Polymer VPP is assigned to ER-142. In that route the post-cured network is the delivered material. ER-149 instead removes the
photoactive organic phase and thermally consolidates powder. Metal binder jetting and bound-metal extrusion belong to ER-147 and
ER-148; they form green geometry by binder placement in a powder bed or by deposition of a pre-compounded road. Ceramic VPP
belongs to ER-151. Polymer-binder powder-bed shaping belongs to ER-155. Laser/electron-beam PBF and DED/WAAM belong to
ER-145, ER-146 and ER-150 because they melt metal during deposition or layer consolidation.
   The industrial selection gate and the direct-versus-indirect route distinction are inherited from ER-139 and ER-049 [11,36]. ER-044
owns photoabsorbing fillers, optical response and cure-depth control; ER-036 owns rheology, recoating and dispersion in highly filled
VPP suspensions; ER-034 owns separation and peel mechanics; ER-031 owns cure shrinkage, residual stress and warpage; and ER-037

owns debinding-defect formation in photopolymer-derived ceramic and metal green bodies [39–43]. ER-149 does not restate those
owners. Its own question is whether a metal-filled, photoactive, layer-delivered system at the loading required for later sintering can
maintain a qualified optical–rheological window through green recovery and then enter a metal-specific debinding/sintering chain without
losing geometry, chemistry, pore-state or factory control. Open-vat oxygen inhibition and stabilisation chemistry are inherited from
ER-030 and ER-032 [37,38]; ER-149 extends them only where metal powder, reservoir history, green conversion and later binder removal
interact. These boundaries preserve the LMM-specific industrial question while preventing duplicate ownership.
   Castable photopolymers for investment casting are not equivalent to powder-loaded LMM. The printed object in a castable route is a
sacrificial pattern, while the final metal is produced by a mould-and-casting chain. The 3Dresyns LMM instructions explicitly distinguish
reactive binder routes intended for debinding/sintering from castable routes intended for jewellery-related indirect manufacture [35]. This
paper uses that page only to define declared workflow scope, never as independent proof of compatibility, performance or safety.
   This review does not prescribe powder chemistry or size, surface treatment, solids loading, binder composition, dispersant, initiator,
absorber, mixing sequence, viscosity, yield stress, temperature, wavelength, irradiance, exposure, layer thickness, recoating speed,
separation motion, cleaning medium, debinding route, furnace atmosphere, thermal ramp, peak temperature, hold, shrink factor, setter
material, HIP cycle or acceptance limit. Each value belongs to a specified powder–binder–light-engine–delivery–geometry–thermal-route
–intended-use state.

distributed as a controlled layer or exposure interface. Patterned

    Traceability crosses batch and load boundaries. One feedstock batch can supply multiple builds; one build can contain multiple
exposure-field positions; one debinding or sintering load can combine parts from several builds; external thermal processing can add

signals constitute acceptance [8,9].
   For purchased components, ISO/ASTM 52901 requires the provider and customer to define feedstock, final characteristics, inspection,
acceptance and documentation  [6]. A purchase order that asks only for “metal DLP 316L” leaves the green and thermal route

test coverage and allowed post-processing.

3. Metal powder, photoactive binder and filled-feedstock release
   The metal powder brings alloy chemistry, particle morphology, size distribution, surface oxide or adsorbates, packing behaviour and
contamination history. The organic phase brings reactive monomer or oligomer, photoinitiator, inhibitors, absorbers, dispersants, diluents,
plasticising or rheology-modifying functions. Their combination is not a neutral carrier around powder: it establishes both the green
network and the chemistry/transport burden that must later be removed.
  ISO/ASTM 52907 structures metal-powder characterisation [12]. Those methods can inform powder identity and condition before
mixing, but do not qualify optical attenuation, dispersion, paste stability, layer formation or debinding. A powder released for PBF, binder

green powder packing and reduce the densification distance. It can also increase viscosity or yield stress, reduce recoating speed, trap air,

window, not one preferred loading.

suspensions that cure depth depended on dispersion/agglomeration, particle size, solids content, refractive index and extinction [20]. The
valid conclusion is coupled optical/material control; the tested values do not transfer to 316L, copper, NiTi or tungsten.
   Dispersion must be tested across scales. A visually uniform reservoir can contain agglomerates, entrained air, settling gradients or
particle/binder segregation. Mixing energy and time can break agglomerates while heating, incorporating gas, changing inhibitor content
or damaging sensitive powder surfaces. Milling media and vessels can add contamination. A controlled batch record defines order of
addition, equipment, atmosphere where relevant, energy/time history, temperature, degassing, filtration or screening, sampling locations
and allowable hold/rework.
   Pan et al. studied dispersant-dependent stability and cure behaviour in a defined 316L slurry [24]. Wu et al. developed a thixotropic
316L paste and linked formulation, stability, cure and final properties in one route [25]. Those studies demonstrate that dispersion,
rheology, light response and thermal conversion can be engineered together. They do not authorise copying the dispersants, loadings,
viscosities, exposure or furnace conditions into another powder, binder or machine.

resist settling at rest but must recover reproducibly after coating shear. Temperature changes viscosity, reaction kinetics and particle
mobility. Repeated circulation, scraping, replenishment or heating can change the mixture. Feedstock release therefore includes a defined
age, container position, conditioning procedure, sampling plan and allowed exposure to light, air and heat.

initiator/inhibitor balance, solvent or cleaning carryover, altered particle distribution and a different light/thermal history. A reuse rule
specifies segregation, screening, refresh ratio where applicable, testing and maximum history. Yield calculations count rejected or
downcycled material rather than labelling all surrounding paste recoverable.

scattering, absorption, agglomeration and spatial composition, so transfer becomes still less defensible.

monochromatic interpretation inadequate [19]. A  light engine must be characterised by spectrum, irradiance,  spatial uniformity,
divergence or numerical-aperture context, focus/distortion and stability at the relevant interface. Their earlier light-engine mapping work
demonstrated position-dependent  irradiance/spectral behaviour and  printed response  in one LCD system  [17]. The  transferable
requirement is registration of a measured optical field, not an assertion that one architecture is uniformly superior.

may fall, while lateral scattering or reflection enlarges a line or closes a gap. Pan et al. quantified pronounced scattering in their studied

exposure is not a universal correction: it can increase lateral overcure, heat, stress, feature closure or adhesion to an interface while still
failing to cure uniformly through a thick, compositionally non-uniform layer.

5. Rheology, sedimentation, layer delivery and material renewal
   ER-036 owns general rheology, recoating and dispersion control for highly filled VPP suspensions [42]. ER-149 narrows the question
to the solids-loading, powder-surface and time-history state needed to leave a sinterable metal skeleton after binder removal.
   Layer formation asks a filled system to flow, level or transfer under a controlled stress and time, then resist sedimentation or drainage
long enough for exposure. A low apparent viscosity can aid renewal but permit settling or edge flow. A high viscosity or yield stress can
retain particles while trapping air, resisting levelling and increasing blade, film or separation loads. Thixotropy can provide both flow
under shear and recovery at rest only if the recovery time matches the machine sequence.
   Rheology must be reported with method, geometry, shear history, temperature and time. A single viscosity at an unspecified shear rate
cannot predict coating. Yield stress inferred by one fitting model may not equal the stress distribution in a doctor blade, gap, roller,
reservoir or moving platform. Oscillatory recovery, creep or step-shear tests can be useful when connected to actual machine events.
Feedstock qualification links these measurements to layer thickness, surface uniformity, particle distribution and green outcomes.
    Material-delivery architectures differ. A liquid-vat route may require bulk recirculation, recoating and separation through a fluid
suspension. A paste route may use a blade, roller, moving carrier or temperature-conditioned transfer. A feedstock that resolidifies or
rebuilds structure between layers may provide green support while increasing renewal and interface sensitivity. The equipment record
declares the architecture instead of using `LMM` as a complete mechanism description.
   Coating creates gradients. Particle migration, wall slip, filtration at a narrow gap, agglomerate exclusion, meniscus behaviour and
evaporation can alter the layer relative to the reservoir. A blade that produces a visually smooth surface can still create local thickness or
composition differences. Temperature across the reservoir, coating element and exposure interface must be mapped where  it affects
rheology or polymerisation.
   Sedimentation control is not proved by a short observation in a static vial. A production job imposes vibration, periodic shear, stops,
replenishment and exposure heat. The qualification interval covers the longest intended dwell, restart and job duration, with samples from
positions that could become powder-rich or binder-rich. Pan et  al. and Wu et  al. provide material-specific examples of stability
engineering [24,25]; their measured times and values remain bounded to their systems.
   Air and volatile content matter. Bubbles can interrupt a layer, scatter light and become green or sintered pores. Vacuum degassing can
remove air while changing volatile composition or accelerating settling. Mixing and recovery from a partially used batch can reintroduce
gas or debris. The work instruction therefore controls degassing endpoint, post-degassing handling and the interval before use.
   Because degassing also changes the oxygen-inhibited induction state, the material-release record includes reservoir headspace,
interface permeability where relevant and the time/shear history by which the feedstock can re-aerate [37,38]. A change in any of those
conditions invokes optical/green-state recalibration; it is not cleared solely by absence of visible bubbles.
   Renewal time contributes to cycle time. Whole-field exposure may illuminate many parts simultaneously, but a larger or more viscous
cross-section can change separation, coating, levelling, temperature and material transport. A thin exposure does not imply a thin factory
cycle. Throughput claims must include the slowest required layer renewal and downstream operation.

7. Green recovery, support claims, cleaning and state release
   The green body must be separated from surrounding unexposed material and the machine interface without cracks, delamination,
bending or surface loss. Green strength depends on binder network, conversion, powder loading, geometry, layer contacts and time. It is a
release property for handling and downstream survival, not a metal performance metric.
   Surrounding suspension or paste can support overhangs during exposure in some architectures. The statement `no printed supports` is
therefore plausible for specified features, but incomplete. Unexposed material must drain, be wiped, displaced or dissolved from surfaces
and internal passages. A narrow, blind, tortuous or closed feature that exposes successfully can fail the cleaning gate. The design file must
provide recovery access and a verifiable cleanliness method.
   Cleaning is a material transformation. Solvent or aqueous contact can extract unreacted species, swell or plasticise the green binder,
mobilise particles, leave residue or cause differential stress. Mechanical wiping or jetting can damage fine features. Drying can create
gradients or surface deposits. A qualified cleaning sequence names the medium, purity, agitation/flow, temperature, time, exchange,
drying and reuse/disposal rules, but this review supplies none of those values.
   Printed green supports, rafts and sacrificial features serve build or handling functions. They can also obstruct cleaning or create
damage during removal. Furnace setters serve a later purpose: supporting the weak brown/sintering body while allowing binder gases and
shrinkage. A green support removed before debinding cannot control sintering sag. A setter that prevents sag can constrain contraction,
mark or contaminate a surface.
   Green inspection includes mass or density where validated, dimensions, surface, visible damage, feature clearance, residual unexposed
feedstock and relevant internal evidence. Bulk green density does not resolve a local agglomerate, binder-rich zone or partially cleaned
cavity. Computed tomography or other imaging may be useful when resolution/contrast are adequate, but a non-detection is not proof
below the method capability.
   Storage and transfer can change the green state. Light, heat, oxygen, humidity and residual solvent can continue reaction or alter
mechanical behaviour. A green part may creep under its own weight or a fixture. Time between printing, cleaning and debinding is
therefore controlled, and transport packaging supports the part without blocking volatile release or adding contamination.
  A green release record identifies build, position, feedstock batch/history, optical state, direct conversion method or declared surrogate,
measurement uncertainty, cleaning lot, inspection result, supports/fixtures, deviations and authorisation to enter debinding. Passing it does
not pre-accept the final metal. It prevents known green defects from entering a furnace load where they become harder and more
expensive to diagnose.

8. Debinding and brown-state control
   ER-037 owns the cross-route thermal-debinding mechanisms, hazard taxonomy and general qualification logic [43]. ER-149 inherits
that framework and narrows this section to the distinctive entry state created by LMM: a particle-filled, spatially non-uniform photocured
network whose crosslinking, cleaning residue, powder/binder distribution and optical history determine transport paths into the brown
state. The industrial task here is to establish that this specific green state can enter the ER-037 framework without concealed conversion
gradients or metal-specific chemistry loss; it is not to duplicate the corpus-wide debinding review.
  A binder may contain fractions intended for water or solvent extraction before thermal pyrolysis. Catalytic or direct thermal routes
may be used in other systems. For an LMM green body these choices begin from an exposure-defined network and are not
interchangeable: compatibility depends on crosslink distribution, powder surface, section thickness, feature openness, cleaning history,
support and furnace state. The 3Dresyns IFU declares separate water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families and explicitly assigns
user validation of the actual solids and workflow [35]. It does not prove that either route is complete or suitable for a particular metal.
   The initial green network can affect debinding beyond total organic mass. Overexposure may increase crosslink density or change
accessibility; undercure can leave weak regions; conversion gradients can create non-uniform decomposition. Cleaning residues can alter
local transport. ER-031 owns general cure-shrinkage, residual-stress and warpage mechanics [40]; the LMM-specific extension is that
shrinkage of a constrained binder around comparatively rigid particles can generate interfacial and packing-scale stress before thermal
shrinkage. That stress can open microcracks, weaken particle bridges or create non-uniform transport paths that later amplify gas-pressure
damage during debinding [22,23,40]. Exposure strategy is therefore a debinding-entry variable because it sets part of the interfacial stress
population on which binder removal acts. A debinding model that begins from nominal binder percentage alone is incomplete.
   Small-sample thermogravimetric or evolved-gas analysis can screen the actual LMM feedstock, but the qualification link is geometry-
and load-specific because optical conversion and cleaning accessibility establish the starting transport field. Roumanie et al. linked
debinding/sintering conditions to copper composition and thermal conductivity in one highly loaded photocurable route [28]. Melentiev et
al. investigated faster crack-free debinding and later sintering of thin-walled 316L metamaterials within a defined system [29]. Their
outcomes remain bounded to those formulations, metals and geometries.
   The brown body can be weaker than the green body after polymer support is lost and before metallurgical necks mature. It can crack
during transfer, setter adjustment or early furnace motion. Some factories may integrate thermal debinding and sintering in one
programme, but the brown transition still exists physically. A defined hold point can rely on mass change, gas response, thermal record,
witness specimens, chemistry or other route-specific evidence.
   The LMM brown-state hold links feedstock batch, spatial conversion or declared surrogate, cleaning state, part section/feature family,
furnace load/location, mass or gas evidence, chemistry and integrity. A completed time–temperature trace alone cannot show that the
photocured network was removed uniformly or that metal chemistry remained acceptable. Binder, powder-surface or conversion changes
also trigger renewed exhaust/condensate and contamination assessment under the ER-037 framework [43].

9. Sintering, shrinkage, setters and dimensional compensation
    Sintering forms metallurgical bonds and reduces pore volume through temperature- and time-dependent transport. Powder chemistry
and surface condition, green packing, residual binder, atmosphere, thermal profile, part geometry, load position and setter interaction
affect densification, grain/phase evolution, chemistry, dimensions and properties. The route is not a low-temperature metal printer
followed by generic firing.
   Shrinkage begins from the spatial green architecture. Local powder fraction, agglomerates, cure and cleaning can vary. During
debinding, organic removal creates pore pathways and may rearrange particles. During sintering, neck growth and pore closure interact
with gravity, thermal gradients and friction. The result can be anisotropic and geometry-dependent even when a nominal bulk scale factor
appears stable.
   Compensation models may include axis factors, local feature offsets, anticipated sag, setter contact and final machining stock. They
are trained on representative parts and load/furnace locations, then tested on independent geometry. A model fitted to one alloy, thickness
or orientation is not a universal machine correction. Any powder, binder, exposure, cleaning, furnace, setter or software change can
invalidate it.
    Setters must carry the part as its stiffness falls and it contracts. A broad contact can resist sag while increasing friction and constraining
in-plane shrinkage. A point or rib support can reduce contact while concentrating load or leaving marks. Setter chemistry, surface, reuse
and contamination are controlled. Sacrificial features and separable powder beds can be considered only after their gas-flow, shrinkage
and cleanliness effects are qualified.
    Pressureless sintering, sinter-HIP, separate HIP, heat treatment and infiltration produce different states. HIP can reduce some internal
porosity but cannot restore a missing feature, remove trapped contamination or automatically correct chemistry. Heat treatment can
change strength or corrosion behaviour without eliminating geometric defects. Reports and drawings name the actual delivered state.
   Copper routes  illustrate atmosphere and chemistry sensitivity. Roumanie et  al. linked thermal conditions to composition and
conductivity [28]; Ye et al. followed a pure-copper slurry route through oxidation, densification and conductivity [33]; Lyu et al. reported
a separate high-resolution copper stereolithography route [34]. These studies are not interchangeable recipes. Their collective lesson is
that final conductivity and density depend on formulation, oxygen/carbon control, pore state and the complete thermal history.
   NiTi creates another boundary. Cohen  et  al. demonstrated sinter-based LMM of a NiTi shape-memory alloy and identified
carbon/phase sensitivity in the tested route [31]. A successful 316L or copper binder and furnace path therefore does not establish NiTi
phase transformation, composition or functional response. The same restriction applies to refractory and reactive materials.
   Dimensional acceptance names the state. Green, cleaned, brown, as-sintered, HIPed, heat-treated, machined and finished dimensions
answer different questions. A drawing and report that omit state make compensation and conformance ambiguous. Stable final dimensions
require part and load evidence, not only a shrinkage percentage from coupons.

10. Material windows, pore state, microstructure and properties
    Metal-filled VPP/LMM has been demonstrated for several material systems, but each result belongs to a particular powder, binder,
optical route, geometry, cleaning and thermal chain. Material breadth is evidence of research possibility, not proof that a shared feedstock
architecture can print `any metal`.
    Stainless-steel 316L has the widest evidence in this source set. Pan et al. coupled slurry preparation, scattering, cure and thermal
conversion [24]. Wu et al. coupled a stable paste with cure and final tensile behaviour [25]. Melentiev et al. demonstrated high-resolution
complex structures [26] and separately examined thin-walled metamaterial debinding/sintering [29]. Pires et al. compared supplied micro-
DLP specimens with binder-jet and laser-fused 316L using microstructure, density, surface and mechanical tests [30]. These results
support multiple viable 316L routes, not one universal density, surface, tensile property or feature limit.
   Comparisons require matched states and specimens. Pires et al. reported differences related to density, surface and grain state, while
noting supplier-proprietary process details and different specimen scales [30]. A micro-tensile specimen, standard coupon and final thin-
walled component do not have identical surface-to-volume ratio, defect sensitivity or test uncertainty. Route ranking without matched
geometry, surface, thermal state and method is weak evidence.
   Copper studies demonstrate optical and thermal challenges without defining one best route. Scheibler et  al. focused on green
cure/strength [27]; Roumanie et al. on debinding/sintering, composition and thermal conductivity [28]; Ye et al. on a pure-copper slurry
route [33]; and Lyu et al. on another stereolithographic process/property window [34]. Powder oxide, organic residue, porosity and
atmosphere can dominate conductivity. A green feature result cannot be converted into final electrical or thermal performance.
   Cai et al. demonstrated DLP processing of tungsten through a water-based precursor and multistage thermal route [32]. The work
broadens the evidence boundary to a refractory metal while remaining formulation-specific. It does not establish that conventional metal-
powder photoresins, debinding cycles or inspection methods transfer to tungsten.
   Density is necessary for many applications but not sufficient. Equivalent bulk density can hide different pore size, shape, connectivity
and location. A surface-connected pore can govern leakage or corrosion; an aligned internal defect can govern fatigue; a closed pore may
respond differently to HIP. Archimedes density, image area fraction and CT have different sampling, resolution and uncertainty.
Acceptance selects methods against the failure mode.
   Microstructure  reflects  the thermal  route.  Sintered 316L can show equiaxed  grains and annealing twins  rather than PBF
melt-pool/cellular structures, as observed in the bounded comparison by Pires et al. [30]. That difference is descriptive, not inherently
superior. Grain size, phase balance, inclusions, carbon/oxygen/nitrogen, porosity and heat treatment must meet intended-use requirements.
   Mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic, corrosion, fatigue, creep or shape-memory claims require state-specific tests. ISO/ASTM
52927 structures main-characteristic and corresponding test-method selection [7]. It does not convert a literature coupon into a product
guarantee. Evidence must include orientation, surface, geometry, environment, sample count, uncertainty and genealogy.

overcure can enlarge a wall while closing a gap. Cleaning can erode a thin wall or leave paste in a channel. Sintering can round, sag or

section or finishing state. Surface measurement reports cutoff/filter, direction, area/line method and whether inaccessible surfaces were
included.

12. Complete-cell productivity, economics, safety and environment
   Exposure time is only one interval in the factory cell. The route includes powder and binder preparation or purchase, sampling,
conditioning, reservoir loading, layer renewal, exposure, separation, part recovery, unexposed-material removal, cleaning, drying, green
inspection, debinding queues, debinding, transfer where applicable, sintering, cooldown, setter removal, heat treatment/HIP where
specified, finishing, cleaning, inspection, rework, scrap and release.
   Effective cell throughput, Tcell = Naccepted / tcomplete-cell, reports accepted components per complete elapsed factory-cell time.
 Material efficiency, ηmaterial = maccepted-parts / mreleased-input, is a separate mass ratio. Neither metric substitutes for the other;
              both declare boundary, period, queue state and disposition of recovered, rejected and downcycled material.
   Whole-field exposure can reduce dependence of exposure time on part count within one image, but nesting, cross-sectional area, layer
renewal, separation and thermal capacity still matter. A full plate of thin parts may expose efficiently and overload cleaning or furnace
fixturing. A single thick component may print successfully and become the debinding bottleneck. Cycle models use accepted yield and
queue capacity rather than ideal exposure speed.
   Feedstock preparation can dominate development or changeover. Mixing, deagglomeration, degassing, stability testing, vat cleaning
and contamination clearance require labour and equipment. Purchased proprietary feedstock can move that burden to the supplier while
increasing supply-chain and equivalence risk. A qualified incoming test remains necessary.
   Recovered unexposed material can reduce waste only when its identity and history remain controlled and it can be reused without
degrading output. Cleaning media, contaminated wipes, cured debris, filters, purge/feedstock residues, failed green parts, debinding
condensate, furnace fixtures and finishing waste remain. Environmental claims require a declared boundary, mass balance, energy/utilities
and accepted yield.
    Printer capital cost is not complete-cell cost. Optical calibration, reservoirs or carriers, coating elements, temperature control, cleaning
equipment, ventilation, solvent/water management, debinding and sintering furnaces, gas supply, setters, metrology, maintenance and
qualified personnel are part of the route. Cost per accepted part includes amortisation, occupancy, consumables, labour, queues, yield loss
and failed qualification.

desktop-VPP guidance identifies dispensing, uncured resin, cleaning, curing and sanding as task-specific control points [15]. Metal
loading adds powder-related hazards during material preparation, spills, d

14. Conclusions and research priorities
   Lithography-based metal manufacturing is not optical metal fusion. It is patterned formation of a metal-filled photopolymer green
body followed by binder removal and metallurgical densification. Its potential for fine geometry and smooth surfaces comes from a
coupled powder–binder–light–layer system whose optical and rheological demands compete. The green object must then be recovered and
cleaned without damage, converted to a porous brown body without internal pressure or residue, and sintered under controlled gravity,
setter and atmosphere conditions.
  A defensible industrial programme follows five rules:
 1. qualify powder, photoreactive binder, additives, mixture and delivery architecture as one time-dependent feedstock system;
 2. measure spectrum, irradiance field, scattering, cure depth, lateral growth and green state instead of transferring wavelength, dose or
    pixel pitch;
 3. keep exposed, cleaned green, brown, sintered, HIPed, heat-treated, machined and delivered states separate;
 4. qualify cleaning access, debinding, shrinkage, setters and final properties on representative geometry and furnace loads; and
 5. compare LMM with other routes using accepted complete-cell throughput, safety, yield and part-linked evidence.
    Priority research should improve in-line dispersion and sedimentation metrology; rheology-to-layer-transfer models for suspension and
paste architectures; three-dimensional light transport in metal-filled media; spatially resolved conversion metrology for highly loaded and
opaque green bodies; validated conversion surrogates with uncertainty and debinding correlation; oxygen/stabiliser and degassing/re-
aeration maps at permeable interfaces; conversion and particle-packing maps; optical-field calibration tied to final geometry; non-
destructive detection of trapped feedstock and green cracks; geometry-aware cleaning and debinding transport; brown-state monitoring;
shrinkage/setter/friction models; small-feature inspection with quantified probability of detection; material-specific chemistry control for
copper, NiTi, tungsten and other advanced metals; and transfer protocols across feedstock batches, machines and furnaces.
    Until those links close for a specified route, claims such as “pixel resolution,” “support-free,” “any metal,” “powder-free,” “safe,”
“zero waste,” “MIM-equivalent,” “fully dense,” “high throughput” and one shrinkage factor remain incomplete. The capability belongs to
a qualified powder–photoactive-binder–layer-delivery–optical–cleaning–thermal–post-process–factory system.

                                                                         2                                                                                  Abstract

   English Abstract
NASA Glenn Research Copper GRCop-42 (Cu-4 at.% Cr-2 at.% Nb) is recognised for its
remarkable strength, creep resistance, and conductivity. It was designed for application in
fusion-based additive manufacturing methods, including powder bed fusion and selective laser
melting. Chromium and Niobium enhance the  material's strength through  precipitation
hardening via the intermetallic phase Cr2Nb. Although Cr2Nb significantly enhances the
properties of GRCop-42, it also impedes pressureless sintering. Consequently, limited research
has been conducted on sinter-based additive manufacturing utilising GRCop-42, as pressureless
solid-state sintering of GRCop-42 is impractical. This study aims to examine whether the
incorporation of additional alloys or elements can facilitate pressureless liquid phase sintering
in GRCop-42 by enhancing wettability. Copper-Tin 90/10 Bronze and Silver were selected.
These should supply adequate liquid phase and capillary force for densification. The disruption
of the stable oxide layer and mass transport via the liquid phase could be accomplished for both
Bronze 90/10 and Silver. In both instances, Cr2Nb underwent dissociation via oxidation owing
to the elevated Oxygen affinity of Niobium. This was induced by trace amounts of water in the
hydrogen sinter atmosphere due to its elevated chemical reactivity. This led to a deterioration
of the wettability of the liquid phase.

                                                                           4                                                                Introduction and Motivation

1.Introduction and Motivation
   1.1. Introduction
Additive manufacturing (AM) has revolutionised a wide range of application technologies,
ranging from ceramics, metallurgy, plastics technologies, all the way to biomedical. The many
different AM methods used today are employed in fields such as manufacturing, defence,
aviation, automotive, healthcare, pharmaceutical industries and many more.[1, 2] Depending
on the application needed, all these sectors can draw upon a plethora of different metal additive
manufacturing (MAM) methods such as binder jetting (BJ), powder bed fusion (PBF), material
extrusion (ME), selective laser sintering (SLS), direct energy deposition (DED) as well as many
more.[3] One of the emerging methods employed in MAM  is Lithography-based Metal
Manufacturing (LMM). It is an attractive alternative which enables the fabrication of small
parts with high resolutions. LMM takes advantage of stereolithography (SLA) and Digital Light
Processing (DLP)  in combination with powder metallurgy.[4] Powder metallurgy  is a
manufacturing technique with a long history dating back to the 1920s.[5] While many MAM
methods frequently produce parts with poor surface and dimensional characteristics, in addition
to limited control over the microstructure, LMM can chiefly eliminate these restrictions. It also
enables the production of parts that require minimal post-treatment.[6] While alloys such as
316L steel have been successfully used for LMM at TU Wien, metals such as Copper and its
alloys are not yet fully developed. Copper is especially useful because it offers a wide range of
applications due to  its high thermal and electrical conductivity.  It is also classified as a
“Strategic Raw Material” by the European Union, which increases the value of manufacturing
techniques such as LMM, which make efficient use of materials.[7] While Copper offers great
conductivity, it lacks mechanical strength. This makes it difficult to use pure copper in high-
tech fields such as aerospace and energy.[8] A remedy to this problem is ternary Copper alloys,
which combine the good properties of Copper with increased mechanical properties such as
creep resistance, low cycle fatigue, as well as strength. This is commonly achieved through
particle-based dispersion strengthening.[9] Although many ternary Copper systems exist, the
most promising in terms of its mechanical capabilities is the Copper-Chromium-Niobium (Cu-
Cr-Nb) system. While a plethora of Cu-Cr-Nb systems with varying amounts of alloying metals
exist, a very common alloy in the field of aerospace is NASA Glenn Research Copper (GRCop),
GRCop-42 (Cu-4 at.% Cr-2 at.% Nb).[8–11] Currently, commonly employed AM techniques
for GRCop-42 are laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) or electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-
PBF), Graded Alloy Processing, and laser powder direct energy deposition (LP-DED).[11–13]
These AM methods all have in common that they do not share the process of sintering found in
classic powder metallurgy as well as LMM processes. No literature could be found which tried
to combine GRCop-42 with LMM and, therefore, atmospheric sintering. The first aim of this
work was to examine whether GRCop-42 could be printed using existing LMM technologies
based on copper LMM applications. The second target was to examine whether GRCop-42
could be sintered using traditional atmospheric sintering methods. This would be needed to
make the combination of GRCop-42 and LMM possible.

2.Theoretical Background
   2.1. LMM
Since its commercial emergence in the second half of the 1980s, additive manufacturing has
made monumental strides in development and production.[14, 15] Since its inception, it has
enabled designers to shift the focus from productibility towards optimal functionality. This has
made AM a vital part of sectors like aerospace, both civilian and military, ranging from aircraft
to  satellites.  Today AM  has  also  reached  sectors  such  as  chemical  engineering,
microelectronics, civil engineering and many more, thanks to its rapid development.[16] In
comparison to other AM methods employed in the sector of metallurgy, such as PBF, SLS,
SLM and Electron Beam Melting (EBM), which often exhibit poor surface characteristics, poor
dimensional accuracy and limited control over the microstructure, Lithography-based additive
manufacturing (LAM) and its derivative LMM have garnered attention as a potential remedy
to these problems.[6] All LAM methods have in common that a photosensitive liquid or
plastically  deformable  photopolymer   is   selectively  cured  through   light-activated
polymerisation. This cured photopolymer then forms a solid 3D object. LAM-based approaches
include SLA  and  DLP.[16–18]  Early  applications  spread  thin  layers  of  monomer,
photoinitiators, and photoabsorbers which were subsequently selectively exposed using a UV
laser. The introduction and use of DLP accelerated production speed,enlarged and expanded
the range and number of products that could be manufactured. Common products were polymer
and ceramic parts made from polymer/ceramic slurries.[16] The introduction of ceramic parts
also introduced another post-processing step. While polymer parts only needed the excess
polymer removed through debinding, ceramics also required sintering. These are the same steps
required for LMM.[16] In recent years, especially micro-3D printing with metals has garnered
wider attention.[4, 7, 16, 19] Owing to the unique characteristics of metals, micro heat
exchangers, 3D circuit boards, 3D electrodes and even movable 3D parts have been printed
using LMM.[20, 21] A whole plethora of variables affect the LMM process which include the
metal powder, the rheology of the feedstock/slurry, photopolymerization, curing depth,
minimum feature size, debinding, sintering and many more.[16] This non-exhaustive list must
be taken into account when considering working with LMM.

   2.2. Liquid phase sintering
With the green part obtained, the next step is sintering. The driving force for sintering is the
reduction of the Gibbs energy ΔG between the initial state and final state of the system. This is
accomplished through the reduction of external (boundary surfaces, walls of pores accessible
from the outside) and internal (walls of enclosed pores, grain boundaries) surfaces. In general,
closely packed particles sinter when being heated near their melting point. As particle size
decreases and the temperature approaches the melting point, sintering speeds up. While smaller
particles result in a larger surface area (bigger difference), heat provides the necessary
activation energy to reduce the Gibbs energy, through the elimination of pores, their rounding
and the coarsening of pores and particles.[22] Sintering is the main method for producing dense,
near-net shape work pieces in powder metallurgy (PM).[23] Two main types of sintering exist:
solid phase sintering and liquid phase sintering (LPS). In LPS, a liquid phase coexists with solid
particles, at high temperature, over a period of time during the sintering process.[22, 24] At the
bare minimum, two chemical elements are required. One element serves as the one which stays
solid, this is the major component and another or several minor components which melt and
promote LPS. These minor components can either melt on their own or form a lower melting
eutectic with the main component.[24] Usually, the solid grains are also soluble (at least to
some extent) in the forming liquid phase.[22] The metal powders used can either be a mixture
of several metal powders or be a pre-alloyed powder, which allows for homogeneous
distribution of the alloying elements throughout the powder.[24] A wide variety of factors
related to the metal powder have an effect on LPS. The size, shape, and distribution of grains
and porosity, along with grain contiguity and connectivity, also play a role in LPS. At the start
of the sintering process, prior to the formation of liquid,
