Continuous heating eventually results in the formation of a liquid phase in and around the
particles. The overall process of LPS can be seen in Figure 3. Three different types of LPS
systems can be distinguished. The first is called supersolidus liquid phase sintering, which is
characterised by the fact that the solid and liquid phases are in chemical equilibrium and that
the amount of liquid phase can be controlled through the sintering temperature and composition.
The solubility ratios between solid and liquid can vary; this leads to the liquid phase either
being present throughout the sintering process, which is called Persistent Liquid Phase (PLP)
sintering, or only for a certain time period, called Transient Liquid Phase (TLP) sintering.
Supersolidus LPS is a special form of PLP. The type of LPS system observed depends on the
chemical equilibrium which is reached at the sintering temperature. If the equilibrium is
reached, then PLP is possible. When it is not reached, the liquid phase will not be present over
the complete  sintering process due  to  it being dissolved  in the solid phase once the
thermodynamic equilibrium is reached. TLP can also occur when one component dissolves in
another, thereby shifting the solidus and liquidus temperatures of the system. If the sintering
temperature is too low, this can make a TLP system out of a PLP one. A characteristic of the
TLP process is chemical inequilibrium in the initial state. In some systems such as Al-Cu, PLP
is combined with TLP. First, TLP breaks the Aluminium oxide layer. Then PLP forms due to
higher temperature, which leads to the desired shrinkage.[24] The solubility plays a vital role
in the rearranging of the particles and therefore the densification of the workpiece. It also affects
the volume of liquid and the time it is present in TLP. In an optimum case, the liquid‐forming
component has low solubility in the solid (main) phase and the solid phase has high solubility
in the liquid-forming phase. Systems which divert from this are less likely to reach maximum
density, since in this optimum, the particles are rearranged through solution-reprecipitation
mechanisms via the liquid phase. Systems which do not correspond to this optimum can
sometimes be improved via the addition of sintering aids such as alloying elements, which
increase the solubility.[24] In TLP systems, the liquid-forming phase frequently has high

Wetting is described through the wetting angle θ, which depends on the equilibrium of the three
surface energies solid‐liquid σSL, liquid‐vapour σLV and vapour‐solid σVS. When the wetting
angle is below 90°, the liquid is considered to be wetting the surface.[24] The wetting liquid
constantly strives to attain the lowest-energy configuration. The low contact angle induces the
liquid  to spread over the  surface, generating  capillary  attraction, which  in turn helps
densification. A broad range of capillary conditions exists due to differences in grain size,
shape, pore size, and overall morphology. When poor wetting occurs, the liquid can retreat from
the solid. This can lead to swelling or the formation of beads on the surface, as pictured in
Figure 5 a).

dissolution, reaction, precipitation, etc. also play a vital role and even overshadow physical

barriers and increasing the contact surface between liquid and solid. Solubility effects can also
strongly enhance the wetting. The control and improvement of wettability are crucial for an
LPS system to work. Wetting can be improved through the modification of the alloy or by using

for rearrangement depends on the particle size and morphology of the solid particles, with small

At the same time, grain growth occurs and can contribute to the closure of large pores and lead

TLP presents an even more complicated system. In comparison to PLP, the activation of the
sintering mechanism through the liquid phase is only possible for a limited time. This is
determined by the dissolution kinetics of the liquid-forming components in the solid phase. A
lot of TLP systems also work with very rigid systems. Comparing this with the high solubility
of the liquid-forming components in the solid phase leads to the aforementioned more
complicated system. A common phenomenon in TLP is the so-called “copper swelling” effect,
which occurs upon the formation and subsequent penetration of the liquid into the interparticle
contacts and grain boundaries, paired with diffusion into the solid particles. TLP is often used
to create strong interparticle contacts and increase the homogenization of the alloying elements
in the microstructure. The described mechanisms do not allow for such high densification as in
PLP. When good wetting occurs in TLP systems, the homogenisation can happen through
eutectic reaction with the base powder and spontaneous melting of the additive particles. This
can be seen in Figure 8 a). In the first instance, the diffusion processes control the formation
and consumption processes of the liquid. Rapid consumption of the liquid near the point of its
inception leads to enrichment of the alloying elements in a certain region but prevents the
distribution throughout the pore network. Small particle sizes of the additives and good mixing
can reduce this effect to some extent. If liquid forms due to spontaneous melting, it is not limited
to the contact points and a higher volume can be formed. In combination with favourable
wetting, this liquid can then distribute throughout the pore network. This can happen with
considerable speed and can be completed before the liquid can be consumed. This mechanism
can be observed in Figure 8 b).

Abstract:
Metal additive manufacturing (AM) enables the production of high value and high performance components1 with applications from aerospace2 to biomedical3 fields. Layer-by-layer fabrication circumvents the geometric limitations of traditional metalworking techniques, allowing topologically optimized parts to be made rapidly and efficiently4,5. Existing AM techniques rely on thermally initiated melting or sintering for part shaping, a costly and material-limited process6–8. We report an AM technique that produces metals and alloys with microscale resolution via vat photopolymerization (VP). Three-dimensional-architected hydrogels are infused with metal precursors, then calcined and reduced to convert the hydrogel scaffolds into miniaturized metal replicas. This approach represents a paradigm shift in VP; the material is selected only after the structure is fabricated. Unlike existing VP strategies, which incorporate target materials or precursors into the photoresin during printing9–11, our method does not require reoptimization of resins and curing parameters for different materials, enabling quick iteration, compositional tuning and the ability to fabricate multimaterials. We demonstrate AM of metals with critical dimensions of approximately 40 µm that are challenging to fabricate by using conventional processes. Such hydrogel-derived metals have highly twinned microstructures and unusually high hardness, providing a pathway to create advanced metallic micromaterials.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) of metals can enable rapid development of advanced parts with complex geometries, opening potential applications in the aerospace, automotive, and biomedical fields. Most existing metal AM techniques rely on costly thermally initiated melting or sintering processes, limiting the fabrication of materials with high thermal conductivity. Alternative vat photopolymerization methods require incorporating target materials or precursors into the photoresin, leading to increased viscosity, light scattering, and the need for a different resin composition for each material fabricated. To circumvent these problems with traditional metal AM techniques, we report an AM process where we infuse aqueous metal precursors into gels formed via vat photopolymerization and subsequently calcine and reduce the gels to form metal structures. Our streamlined technique enables the use of a single photoresin composition and varied post-processing conditions to fabricate a wide variety of metals and alloys with microscale resolution and highly twinned microstructures. We demonstrate fabrication of microlattices with <50 µm beam diameters formed from copper, nickel, silver, and alloys thereof, as well as high entropy and refractory alloys. We found that during the calcination process, the rate of mass loss associated with the exothermic combustion of the gel scaffold must be controlled to form dense parts. Microcrystalline microstructures with crystallographic annealing twin densities on the order of 10<jats:sup>6 </jats:sup>m<jats:sup>-1 </jats:sup>were achieved. Our simple and compositionally flexible hydrogel-based approach to metal AM provides a pathway to fabricate new classes of metals with non-equilibrium microstructures and enhanced properties. Furthermore, our method is compatible with commercially successful vat photopolymerization techniques, showing a clear path to widespread adoption of this technique.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000015

From text 'saccone2022additivemanufacturingof pages 1-2'.

Max A. Saccone, Rebecca A. Gallivan, Kai Narita, Daryl W. Yee, and Julia R. Greer. Additive manufacturing of micro-architected metals via hydrogel infusion. Nature, 612:685-690, Oct 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05433-2, doi:10.1038/s41586-022-05433-2. This article has 258 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

Hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM) is a vat-photopolymerization metal-printing method developed by the Caltech team including Julia R. Greer. First, digital light processing (DLP) prints a three-dimensional organogel scaffold from a DMF/PEGda photoresin; this printing step defines the final geometry. Photoactive compounds are leached out, the structure undergoes solvent exchange and swelling, and an aqueous metal precursor infiltrates the hydrogel. Calcination in air removes the polymer and forms a metal-oxide replica, which is then reduced in forming gas to produce the metal or alloy. Because material is introduced after shaping, the same photoresin can support different compositions without reoptimizing the resin and curing parameters, enabling compositional tuning and multimaterials. Demonstrated materials include copper, silver, nickel, CuNi, the high-entropy alloy CuNiCoFe, refractory W–Ni, and a Cu/Co multimaterial gradient. The reported critical feature dimensions are approximately 40 micrometres. The resulting hydrogel-derived metals possess highly twinned microstructures and unusually high hardness, although the excerpt does not provide numerical hardness values or broader mechanical-property data. The Greer group’s contribution, as represented by this work, was the development and demonstration of HIAM for architected metallic microlattices and alloys at microscale resolution.

KG Priority Date 2015-11-10 Filing Date 2016-11-10 Publication Date 2017-05-18 Keywords metal, slurry, μιη, radiation, coo DEFINITIONS the invention relates to a an additive manufacturing method, more particularly indirect stereolithography (SLA) or dynamic light processing (DLP), for the production of three- dimensional metal objects. SLA indirect stereolithography DLP dynamic light processing the invention further relates to a slurry for use in said additive manufacturing method and to three- dimensional metal objects obtainable by said additive manufacturing method.additive manufacturing is a process, usually a layer-by- layer process, of joining materials to make objects from a three-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD) data model. CAD computer-aided design the applications of additive manufacturing processes have been expanding rapidly over the last 20 years. additive manufacturing processes are material jetting, material extrusion, direct energy deposition, sheet lamination, binder jetting, powder bed fusion and photopolymerization. These technologies can all be applied to shape ceramic or metal components, starting from (sub)micro meter-sized ceramic or metal particles. AM processes There are basically two diﬀerent categories of AM processes: (i) single-step processes (also called 'direct' processes), in which three-dimensional objects are fabricated in a single operation where the basic geometrical shape and the basic material properties of the intended product are achieved simultaneously and (ii) multi-step processes (also called 'indirect' processes), in which three-dimensional objects are fabricated in two or more steps wherein the ﬁrst step typically provides the basic geometric shape and the following steps consolidate the product to the intended material properties. single-step processes also called 'direct' processes multi-step processes also called 'indirect' processes the present invention concerns an indirect AM process which makes use of a sacriﬁcial binder material to shape solid powder particles. Said binder material is obtained using photopolymerization of a polymerizable resin and a polymerization photoinitiator contained in a slurry which also contains the solid powder particles. the sacriﬁcial binder material is removed in a subsequent 'debinding' treatment. Examples of the process according to the present invention are indirect stereolithography (SLA), Digital Light Processing (DLP) and Large Area Maskless Photopolymerization (LAMP). US6, 117,612 concerns stereo lithographic resins for rapid prototyping of ceramics and metals. US6, 117,612 discloses photo-curable ceramic resins having solids loadings in excess of 40 vol% and a viscosity of less than 3000 mPa-s and their use in multi-layer fabrication of green ceramic parts. the photo-curable resins can also contain sinterable metals. the depth of cure of the resin is equal to or larger than the thickness of each layer such that the interface between the layers in suﬃciently cured in order to provide the three-dimensional object with suﬃcient mechanical strength. the penetration depth of the radiation that is used to activate the polymerization photo initiator must be larger than the thickness of the layer.the depth of cure depends upon factors related to the photopolymerization itself, including the monomer concentration, the nature and concentration of the photoinitiator, and the dose of radiation. Factors related to the ceramic or metal powder are also important. For transparent powders, the depth of cure is largely determined by scattering of the radiation and by the volume fraction of the particles. Abstract:
PURPOSE
This review aims to summarize the available technologies, material categories, and prosthodontic applications of additive manufacturing (AM) dental ceramics, evaluate the achievable accuracy and mechanical properties in comparison with current mainstream computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing (CAD/CAM) subtractive manufacturing (SM) methods, and discuss future prospects and directions.


STUDY SELECTION
This paper is based on the latest reviews, state-of-the-art research, and existing ISO standards on AM technologies and prosthodontic applications of dental ceramics. PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect were amongst the sources searched for narrative reviews.


RESULTS
Relatively few AM technologies are available and their applications are limited to crowns and fixed partial dentures. Although the accuracy and strength of AM dental ceramics are comparable to those of SM, they have the limitations of relatively inferior curved surface accuracy and low strength reliability. Furthermore, functionally graded additive manufacturing (FGAM), a potential direction for AM, enables the realization of biomimetic structures, such as natural teeth; however, specific studies are currently lacking.


CONCLUSIONS
AM dental ceramics are not sufficiently developed for large-scale clinical applications. However, with additional research, it may be possible for AM to replace SM as the mainstream manufacturing technology for ceramic restorations.

Ceramics, known for their heat resistance, hardness, wear resistance, and electrical insulation properties, are particularly suited for aerospace, automotive, electronics, healthcare, and energy applications. The rise of 3D printing in ceramics has opened new possibilities, allowing the fabrication of complex structures and the use of diverse raw materials, overcoming the limitations of conventional fabrication methods. Abstract:
<jats:p>This study evaluates the rapid tooling feasibility and structural significance of utilizing digital light processing (DLP)-printed alumina as a near-net-shape ceramic mold-insert preform route for replication of curved polymer optics. While conventional production tooling for precision optics demands immediate optical-grade tolerances, the fundamental mechanisms governing polymer replication close to additively manufactured ceramic interfaces remain insufficiently understood. To isolate these multi-factor processing signatures, alumina specimens incorporating concave and convex parabolic surfaces were synthesized via lithography-based ceramic manufacturing. Our design acts as a geometric control lens, ensuring that thermal shrinkage trends, slicing kinematics, and interfacial replication behaviors are clearly exposed and quantified under uniform boundary conditions. Following debinding and sintering, exploratory hot-pressing cycles were executed to evaluate gross profile transfer and surface inheritance on poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) replicas. Quantitative laser scanning confocal microscopy confirmed successful gross curvature generation and revealed geometry-dependent post-sintering shrinkage trends. The convex inserts exhibited an average peak-to-valley (PV) error of 123.48 ± 3.30 µm and an RMS error of 29.76 ± 1.23 µm, whereas the concave alumina inserts showed an average PV error of 137.98 ± 5.80 µm and an RMS error of 34.68 ± 1.20 µm. The PMMA replicas also showed substantial form deviation, with an average PV error of 163.72 ± 15.64 µm and RMS error of 27.37 ± 2.03 µm. Our work presents a route for producing near-net-shape ceramic mold-insert preforms that transforms complex processing variations into a predictable, mathematically addressable roadmap. A geometry-specific CAD pre-compensation can then be performed while the remaining precision gap can be selectively closed via targeted post-polishing depending on the desired optical application tier.</jats:p>

## 1. segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 1-2 (Context ID: pqac-00000028)

                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139

A State-Resolved Framework for Industrial Additive-Manufacturing
Technology Selection Across Polymers, Metals, Ceramics and Advanced
Materials
Process Chains, Invalidation Gates, Factory Constraints and Qualification

Juan Segurola
3Dresyns by Resyner Technologies S.L.
Registered tax address: General Etxague 15B, 20003 Donostia / San Sebastián, Gipuzkoa, Spain
VAT number: ESB24827511
Correspondence: [email redacted] · Website: www.3Dresyns.com
ER-139 · Engineering Review · Version 0.3 · 2 September 2026

Statement of Significance
   Additive-manufacturing technologies are often compared through machine-level descriptors such as nominal resolution, build
rate, material label or purchase price. Those descriptors do not identify the state of the object leaving the machine or the operations
required before it becomes an accepted component. A photopolymer object may still require washing and post-cure; a metal or
ceramic green body may require debinding and sintering; a powder-bed component may remain unusable until it can be recovered
and verified; and a deposited metal form may require machining and interface qualification. ER-139 establishes a state-resolved
selection framework that links process category, feedstock, geometry, scale, orientation, shaping mechanism, recovery, mandatory
transformations, factory resources, economics and intended-use evidence. It also supplies a documented output record and a
worked screening example. Its central rule is that an additive route has no unconditional advantage: a benefit is meaningful only
against a declared comparator and within a controlled material-process-workflow-factory state.
Keywords: additive manufacturing; process selection; material extrusion; powder bed fusion; vat photopolymerisation; binder jetting;
material jetting; directed energy deposition; solid-state deposition; sheet lamination; polymers; metals; ceramics; advanced materials;
post-processing; factory qualification

Abbreviations: AM, additive manufacturing; AFSD, additive friction stir deposition; DED, directed energy deposition; DIW, direct ink
writing; ESD, electrostatic discharge; LMM, lithography metal manufacturing; PBF, powder bed fusion; UAM, ultrasonic additive
manufacturing; VPP, vat photopolymerisation; WAAM, wire-arc additive manufacturing.

Abstract
    Industrial additive manufacturing spans seven standard process categories and a growing set of adjacent, non-layerwise, direct,
indirect and hybrid implementations. Category names alone do not identify the state of the object leaving the machine, the
transformations needed to obtain a usable component or the factory evidence required for repeatable production. This qualitative
engineering review develops a state-resolved framework for screening additive-manufacturing routes across polymers, metals,
ceramics and advanced materials. It separates feedstock state, shape-creation mechanism, usable scale and orientation, support or
depowdering strategy, as-built state, mandatory post-processing, delivered material state and intended-use qualification. The seven
categories are mapped together with exposure-architecture, indirect-tooling, functional-material and adjacent solid-state-deposition
overlays. The comparison addresses geometry, throughput, material utilisation, labour, safety, surface state, anisotropy, shrinkage,
inspection and economics without assigning universal scores. Representative primary studies show why raster direction, powder
history, exposure architecture, droplet waveform, melt-pool regime, green-body processing, particle impact, thermomechanical
deposition, thermal history and support environment remain route-specific. The decision gate begins with the required delivered
state and works backward through the complete process chain. A worked ceramic example shows how the framework records
candidate routes, invalidation gates, evidence gaps, provisional survivors and no-go rationale. The framework supports route
screening, experimental planning and qualification design;  it does not replace application-specific costing, process validation,
regulatory assessment or production-site qualification.

1. Purpose, scope and objectives
   The selection question addressed here is not "which printer is best?" It is: which controlled production route can deliver the
required geometry, material state and function at an acceptable factory burden, with evidence suitable for the intended
use? ISO/ASTM 52900:2021  supplies a common vocabulary  for AM  processes, while ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 frames
requirements for industrial processes and production sites [1,2]. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
likewise treats material, machine, process, post-process measurement and part qualification as connected problems [5-7].
   ER-139 covers polymers, metals, ceramics, glasses, reinforced systems, nano/micron-filled composites and highly specialised
resins at component-relevant scales. Construction, concrete, geopolymer, regolith and other macroscopic high-volume deposition
routes are outside scope. Current 3Dresyns portfolio pages distinguish nano/micron raw materials from ready-to-print specialty
resins; they define the declared scope of later specialist reviews but are not independent evidence of performance [32,33].
   The objectives are to:
 1. establish a common state-resolved record for comparing direct, indirect, hybrid and adjacent AM routes;

                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139 · 2026 · Page 1

                                          © 2026 Juan Segurola. All Rights Reserved.                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139


 2. identify material, geometry, scale, recovery, transformation, safety, economic and qualification conditions that can invalidate a route
     before machine-level optimisation;
 3. distinguish mechanistic, demonstrated and factory advantages so that evidence is not transferred beyond its tested boundary; and
 4. define a compact selection output that preserves surviving routes, evidence gaps and no-go rationale for later experiments and change
     control.
   The paper does not rank vendors, pool numerical properties across incompatible machines or assign universal values for speed,
accuracy, density, cost or sustainability. Green, as-built, washed, post-cured, debound, sintered, heat-treated, machined and
conditioned specimens remain distinct evidence states.

2. Why the category name is necessary but insufficient
   The seven ISO/ASTM categories identify the primary shaping mechanism, but an industrial route requires more variables. The
minimum route description is:
   R = {feedstock and lot history; machine state; geometry, scale, orientation and build plan; shaping mechanism; recovery;
                       mandatory transformations; measurement; delivered state; intended use}.
   Changing one member can alter the process window or invalidate an earlier comparison. A resin swap can change exposure
depth and washing. A powder reuse policy can change flow, packing or thermal history. A new geometry or orientation can change
heat accumulation, support demand, recovery and measurement access. A furnace change can alter debinding, atmosphere,
dimensional evolution and final microstructure. The category is therefore an entry point, not a selection result.

   Five overlays complete the route record. First, exposure architecture distinguishes scanned, projected, masked, continuous,
tomographic and highly localised routes without promoting every implementation to a separate category. Continuous liquid-
interface production changes the exposure-transport boundary but retains formulation, conversion and final-property controls [10].
Second, this review uses three explicit route conventions. In a direct route, the printed object supplies the material of the delivered
part, although conditioning may remain. In an indirect route, the printed object is a green preform, pattern, mould, core or
sacrificial tool that is materially transformed, consumed or removed. In an integrated hybrid route, additive and non-additive
operations alternate inside one controlled chain, for example deposition interleaved with measurement and machining. This differs
from an external comparator such as a wholly machined or moulded route. Third, every candidate needs a state-transformation
record. Fourth, a functional-material overlay is required for conductive, ESD, dielectric, magnetic, optical, radiation-functional,
adaptive and soft systems because shape fidelity does not establish service function. Fifth, adjacent solid-state metal-deposition
routes are recorded by their mechanism and delivered state even when an exact placement in the seven-category taxonomy is not
asserted.

3. The feedstock-to-delivered-part chain
   Figure 1 defines the minimum object-state chain. "As printed" is a final state only when no mandatory transformation remains
and acceptance evidence is valid in that state.





                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139 · 2026 · Page 2                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139





                                                  Figure 1. State-resolved production chain
   Polymer material extrusion can produce the final polymer chemistry directly, yet bead orientation and interlayer formation
remain part of the material state. Ahn et  al. demonstrated direction- and process-variable dependence in one acrylonitrile-
butadiene-styrene system; that result establishes an anisotropy gate, not a transferable percentage [8]. Polymer PBF may avoid
separate supports for many geometries, but powder history and thermal exposure remain consequential. Vendittoli et al. reported
changes in reused polyamide 12 powder and parts within their selective-laser-sintering workflow, supporting lot-history and
refresh-policy controls without defining a universal reuse limit [9].
   Photopolymerisation transfers another set of variables. Cured geometry depends on absorption, scattering, exposure, separation
and transport, while the delivered network depends on washing, post-cure and conditioning. Filled photopolymers intensify the
coupling: particles alter viscosity, sedimentation, scattering and cure depth, while the binder must either remain as a composite
phase or be removed without damaging a green body.
   In metal and ceramic sinter-based routes, the printer intentionally creates an intermediate. Bound-metal extrusion, binder jetting
and LMM all require a green-to-final transformation, but their green structures arise by different mechanisms. Shima et al. linked
deposition and densification to microstructure and tensile behaviour in a specific 17-4PH bound-metal workflow [14]. Chen et al.
and Cabo Rios et al. showed that binder-jet printing conditions and sintering can control densification and directional dimensional
evolution in 316L systems [15,16]. LMM studies likewise separate suspension preparation and cure from debinding and sintering
[17,18]. Final-metal properties therefore cannot be assigned to the printed green state, and nominally identical furnace schedules
are not presumed transferable across green-body architectures.

4. Material-class eligibility and invalidation gates
   Material class narrows route eligibility, but labels such as polymer, metal or ceramic remain too broad. A thermoplastic melt, a

deposition deformation and the fired ceramic outcome in one boehmite-derived alumina system [22]. The transferable logic is

causal: the ink must flow through the nozzle, recover sufficient structure, dry without unacceptable damage and survive thermal
conversion. The study's numerical criteria remain specific to that ink and test configuration.
   Glass-forming routes impose a similar boundary. Kotz et al. demonstrated that a photocurable nanocomposite can be shaped
and thermally converted into fused-silica structures [23]. That evidence supports a multistage route, not the claim that any silica-
filled resin will become transparent glass. Particle identity, loading, dispersion, organic removal, shrinkage, bubbles and thermal
history belong to the delivered optical material.
   Reinforced and soft systems show different transition risks. Matsuzaki et al. used in-nozzle impregnation to print continuous-
fibre composites, making reinforcement path and interface formation explicit variables [24]. Hinton et al. used a reversible support
bath to stabilise complex hydrogel geometries [25]. In each case, the environment surrounding deposition is part of the route;
demonstration of shape retention is not long-term mechanical, biological or service qualification.

5. Conditional advantages and process-specific losses
  An advantage should be assigned to one of three levels. A mechanistic advantage follows from the shaping principle. A
demonstrated advantage requires matched evidence for the material, machine, geometry and workflow. A factory advantage
requires accepted-part throughput, labour, yield and cell-cost evidence. Without a comparator and boundary, the statement remains
an unresolved claim.
5.1 Polymer-dominant routes
   Material extrusion can place material selectively with comparatively simple feedstock handling and can scale from fine
filament deposition to high-flow pellet systems. Its mechanistic losses include bead-scale surface texture, direction-dependent
interfaces, start/stop defects, thermal gradients and support-access constraints. Larger nozzles may improve volumetric deposition
while sacrificing feature access and surface state; smaller nozzles reverse that trade-off.
   Polymer PBF uses surrounding powder as geometric support for many features and permits three-dimensional batch nesting.

5.1 Polymer-dominant routes
   Material extrusion can place material selectively with comparatively simple feedstock handling and can scale from fine
filament deposition to high-flow pellet systems. Its mechanistic losses include bead-scale surface texture, direction-dependent
interfaces, start/stop defects, thermal gradients and support-access constraints. Larger nozzles may improve volumetric deposition
while sacrificing feature access and surface state; smaller nozzles reverse that trade-off.
   Polymer PBF uses surrounding powder as geometric support for many features and permits three-dimensional batch nesting.
The complete cycle includes bed preparation, heating, building, cooling, excavation, depowdering, powder segregation or refresh
and surface finishing. Internal channels can be geometrically printable yet operationally unacceptable if powder cannot be removed
or verified.
  VPP can localise cure through scanning, projection or masking and can provide fine exposure-defined features. Its losses
include support contact, separation forces, residual liquid, washing, post-cure, oxygen or optical effects and conversion gradients.
Continuous exposure can alter vertical transport and machine occupancy [10], but speed remains geometry-, resin- and acceptance-
dependent. Material jetting offers spatial placement and multimaterial potential, yet the result depends on droplet formation,
temperature, rheology, waveform, nozzle condition and support strategy. Chen et al. demonstrated that coupling in one waveform-
modelled material-jetting system [11]; its operating window is not a generic printhead or ink specification.
5.2 Fusion, sinter-based and solid-state metal routes
   Laser PBF (L-PBF) can create complex metal geometries through local melting, but  it combines powder handling, rapid
thermal  cycling, support  design,  residual  stress, surface roughness and  internal-defect  control.  Ultrafast X-ray work by
Cunningham et  al. linked pore formation to a keyhole-regime transition in a bounded laser-melting experiment [12]. The
transferable lesson is that nominal energy density does not replace control of the melt regime. Electron-beam PBF (EB-PBF)
changes the energy source, vacuum environment and preheat strategy; Al-Bermani et al. linked thermal history to microstructural
diversity and properties in Ti-6Al-4V [13].
  DED and WAAM can add material to existing components, repair local regions and generate large near-net forms. Their
conditional benefit is deposition access and material addition where fine powder-bed feature control may not be the objective.
Their losses include high heat input, thermal accumulation, residual stress, deformation, coarse surface state and machining
allowance. Carroll et al. reported directional tensile behaviour in DED Ti-6Al-4V [26], while Ma et al. treated scanning strategy as
a control variable for stress and deformation in one WAAM Al-Si system [27].
   Binder jetting, bound-metal extrusion and LMM move much of the consolidation burden from the printer to debinding and
sintering. This can reduce melt-related thermal stress during shaping and enable batch furnace processing, but it creates a fragile
intermediate,  dimensional  transformation,  furnace  loading  constraints and  risks from  binder  removal,  atmosphere and
contamination. Binder jetting adds green-part excavation; bound extrusion adds bead interfaces and green anisotropy; LMM
couples metal loading to suspension flow and optical cure. Output must be measured after sintering and final acceptance.
    Solid-state metal deposition changes the governing invalidation gates because consolidation proceeds without intentional bulk
melting. In cold-spray AM, powder morphology and native particle state interact with particle flight, impact conditions, bonding
and deposited properties. Anumandla et al. demonstrated those couplings for commercially pure titanium powders of different
manufacture and morphology [34]. A candidate route therefore needs controls for powder identity, particle-size and shape
distributions, gas and nozzle conditions, substrate preparation, interparticle and substrate bonding, deposited defects and any
finishing required; absence of melting does not itself prove an acceptable interface or property state.
  AFSD uses thermomechanical deformation and plastic flow rather than local melting and solidification. Kincaid et  al.
combined AFSD with structured-light measurement, turning and milling in two manufacturing demonstrations [35]. Their work
shows why a near-net deposit that requires measurement and machining is an integrated hybrid chain: coordinate transfer, datum
strategy, deposition allowance, tool access and operation sequence contribute directly to the accepted geometry. Cold spray and


                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139 · 2026 · Page 4                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139


AFSD are retained here as adjacent solid-state metal-deposition routes and are not forced into an unverified exact position within
the seven-category taxonomy.
   Sheet lamination occupies another solid-state boundary. UAM bonds metal foils at relatively low bulk temperature and can
embed temperature-sensitive elements. Hehr et al. demonstrated integration of fibre-optic strain sensors within metal using UAM
[28]. This establishes an opportunity under the studied conditions, not general production qualification; interface, foil, geometry,
machining and sensor-survival evidence remain necessary.
5.3 Advanced and highly specialised materials
   Nano/micron feedstocks should be classified by physical form, chemistry, surface state, dispersion route and whether the
particulate phase remains in the component. A nanopowder, agglomerate, nanofibre, micronised powder, concentrate and ready-to-
print resin are not interchangeable. For a retained composite, particle distribution, interface state, orientation and percolation may
control function. For an indirect metal, ceramic or glass route, the carrier must be removed and the particles consolidated; final
function belongs to the transformed structure, not the wet formulation.
   Highly specialised resins should be selected from service state backward. Electrical or ESD materials require geometry-specific
resistance and contact evidence. Thermally conductive systems require direction, interface and boundary-condition control.
Dielectric, ferroelectric, piezoelectric and magnetic systems may require alignment, poling or field-history records. Optical,
photonic, luminescent and radiation-functional systems require spectral, attenuation, dose or energy definitions. Extreme-service
resins require the actual temperature, chemical, flame, barrier or insulation test. Adaptive and soft systems require activation,
recovery, fatigue, solvent or humidity state. These topics are assigned to ER-156-ER-161; ER-139 defines their common selection
boundary.

6. Factory-cell constraints and occupational safety
   The factory cell comprises every resource needed to convert feedstock into an accepted component. A printer cannot be
evaluated separately from material storage, atmosphere, recovery, cleaning, curing, furnaces, machining, ventilation, waste
handling, metrology, maintenance and operator competence.

   Safety evidence must be bounded by task and facility. In a 2025 National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
evaluation of one metal-powder AM facility, airborne particles increased during tasks, metals were detected in breathing zones and
on surfaces, skin and clothing, and feedstock powder migrated through production and non-production areas; measured breathing-
zone values were below the applicable occupational exposure limits in that facility [29]. This facility-specific result shows why
powder transfer, depowdering, cleaning, maintenance and transport belong in the process map; it does not establish another site's
exposure or compliance.
   For desktop VPP, NIOSH identifies uncured resin, acrylates, cleaning solvents, curing emissions and sanding dust as exposure-
control topics and recommends appropriate ventilation, handling and personal protection [30]. Nano/micron materials require
separate hazard and exposure assessment based on composition and physical form. Current NIOSH nanotechnology guidance
directs users to containment, engineering-control, sampling and material-specific resources rather than treating "nano" as one
hazard class [31]. Particle size alone neither proves nor excludes risk.

7. Economics without marketing shortcuts
   The primary production denominator is accepted output from the complete cell:


                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139 · 2026 · Page 5                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139


 Effective cell throughput = accepted components delivered / observation period, measured at steady state for the declared batch
                                            mix and utilisation.
   Lead time is separate: it is the elapsed time from released feedstock to final acceptance for one batch. In a pipelined cell,
steady-state throughput is controlled by the bottleneck stage rather than by the sum of one batch's stage times. Printer output, lead
time and cell throughput must therefore be reported independently.
   The  cost boundary  includes equipment occupancy,  labour,  feedstock  loss,  reusable  fractions, consumables,  utilities,
atmosphere, supports, cleaning, post-processing, inspection, maintenance, rework, scrap and failed qualification. A route may have
low marginal geometry cost but high recovery labour; high printer output but a furnace bottleneck; good material utilisation but
costly containment; or rapid green-part output followed by low final yield.
   Comparisons should freeze annual volume, part mix, geometry, acceptance criteria, utilisation, queue model and comparator.
Machining, moulding, casting and a separately defined integrated hybrid chain are legitimate comparators when they deliver the
same accepted state. AM should not receive credit for unused geometric freedom or customisation, and the comparator should not
be burdened with tooling or inventory assumptions absent from the actual case.
   Environmental claims require the same boundary discipline. "Less waste" may describe near-net placement while omitting
supports, unrecoverable powder, solvents, inert gas, furnaces, failed parts or machining. This framework retains energy and
material flow as case variables but assigns no universal sustainability rank.

8. Qualification architecture and change control
  ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 separates industrial-process and production-site requirements from the claim that a particular part is
qualified [2]. ISO/ASTM 52927:2024 maps main AM characteristics to corresponding test methods, while ISO/ASTM 52928:2024
addresses metal-powder life-cycle management [3,4]. These standards help structure controlled records; they do not replace
application-specific acceptance criteria.
  A minimum qualification architecture contains:
 1. Feedstock record: identity, supplier or preparation route, lot, storage, age, conditioning, reuse or blending history, and process-
     controlling properties.
 2. Machine-state record: configuration, software and parameter set, calibration, maintenance, critical consumables, atmosphere and
     pre-build checks.
 3. Build record: geometry revision, scale check, orientation, nesting, supports, exposure or deposition history, interruptions and in-
     process evidence.
 4. Transition record: recovery, washing, cure, drying, debinding, sintering, infiltration, heat treatment, machining, polishing and
     conditioning, including equipment identity and load configuration.
 5. Measurement record: traceable dimensional, surface,  internal-defect, composition, microstructure, mechanical or functional
     evidence with uncertainty appropriate to the decision.
 6. Acceptance record: intended use, critical characteristics, direct-inspection or validated indirect-verification strategy, sampling logic,
    non-conformance disposition and linkage between specimens and production parts.
 7. Change-control record: rules for reassessing material, machine, geometry, parameters, post-process equipment, site, software or
     inspection changes.
   NIST's part-qualification programme highlights measurement challenges created by complex surfaces and internal geometry,
defects, anisotropy, residual stress and post-processing [7]. Those challenges make "same material and printer" an inadequate
equivalence argument. Qualification should follow the causal route from feedstock and machine state to the features that control
final performance.

P Mastny. High-strength copper alloys for indirect additive manufacturing using photolithography. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt provides only partial specifications for the Incus Hammer Lab35 and does not describe Admaflex printers. This avoids designing a separate particle-loaded slurry or hybrid resin for every composition and enables compositional flexibility, including refractory metals, high-entropy alloys, and multimaterial structures. For metal fabrication, the infused metal salts occupy the hydrogel/polymer network, are converted during thermal treatment into metal oxides, and are subsequently reduced with hydrogen gas to form metals or alloys. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Barrier | Description | Evidence source |
|---|---|---|
| Part size and wall thickness | The process is best suited to small, intricate parts. Thick or closed sections lengthen binder-transport paths and raise cracking, residue, distortion, and inspection risks. Minimum printable walls also differ from minimum cleanable gaps or channels; projector pixel pitch is not final-part resolution. Published limits are machine-, alloy-, orientation-, and geometry-specific rather than universal. | Segurola identifies small intricate components as the opportunity and thick or closed regions as the controlling liability; it requires final-state feature mapping rather than reliance on pixel pitch. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) |
| Cure–loading trade-off | Higher metal loading reduces binder content and sintering distance but increases viscosity, agglomeration, settling, and optical attenuation. Lower loading improves flow and cure depth but increases organic-removal burden and shrinkage. Copper experiments show cure thickness and green strength depend jointly on loading, particle size, exposure, and orientation. | Segurola’s review synthesizes the coupled optical–rheological trade-off and cites Scheibler et al.’s 2024 copper study. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009) |
| Feedstock availability and alloy transferability | A powder qualified for MIM, LPBF, binder jetting, or extrusion is not automatically suitable for metal VPP: surface chemistry, oxide state, particle size, dispersion, optical response, and rheology all matter. Commercial feedstocks cover only a limited set of qualified alloys, and each powder–binder–printer–furnace combination needs validation. Incus literature documents successful 316L and copper processing, not universal metal compatibility. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000033) |
| Cleaning and debinding | Surrounding uncured feedstock must be removed from surfaces and internal passages without eroding fragile green features. Blind, narrow, or tortuous channels may print successfully yet fail cleaning. During debinding, gas evolution and long transport paths can cause cracks, blisters, delamination, residue, or chemistry changes; the brown body may be weaker than the green body. | Incus processing involves decaking, solvent cleaning, solvent debinding, thermal debinding, and sintering; Segurola treats cleanability and geometry-specific debinding as separate qualification gates. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000043) |
| Shrinkage and dimensional control | Shrinkage is anisotropic and geometry-, orientation-, packing-, furnace-load-, and setter-dependent. A single isotropic scale factor cannot reliably compensate walls, holes, lattices, and massive sections. Setters reduce sag but can constrain contraction, mark surfaces, or introduce contamination. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008) |
| Reactive and precipitation-strengthened alloys | Alloys optimized for fusion AM may sinter poorly. For example, Cr₂Nb strengthens GRCop-42 but pins boundaries and inhibits pressureless densification; Cr/Nb oxides and trace water in hydrogen can impair wetting and disrupt phases. This is directly relevant to Cu–Cr–Zr, Cu–Cr–Nb, Al–Zr, and similar oxide-sensitive development programs. | Mastny’s GRCop-42 study found pressureless solid-state sintering impractical without additional liquid-phase strategies and documented oxide and wetting sensitivity. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |
| Qualification and standards | ISO/ASTM 52900 classifies the shaping step as vat photopolymerization, but the delivered product is a sintered metal part. Applicable frameworks include ISO/ASTM 52901, 52907, 52920, 52927, 52931, 52951, and 52953. These organize purchasing, powder characterization, site qualification, testing, safety, and data—not alloy-specific acceptance. MPIF Standard 35 remains a useful MIM/property comparator, but it does not qualify an LMM process or its dimensional capability. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) |
| Competition from binder jetting | Binder jetting generally offers larger build envelopes, three-dimensional nesting, broader industrial powder ecosystems, and high green-part throughput. Its disadvantages are depowdering, lower green strength, binder-placement resolution, and the same furnace and shrinkage burden. Metal VPP competes where finer surfaces and smaller features justify lower scale and more difficult slurry handling. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031) |
| Competition from micro-LPBF | Micro-LPBF directly consolidates metal and avoids cleaning uncured resin plus debinding, but carries melt-pool, support, residual-stress, reflectivity, thermal-distortion, powder-safety, and surface-roughness burdens. Metal VPP is attractive for reflective copper and fine, smooth batches, but only if sintering preserves chemistry, density, and dimensions. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000031) |
| Competition from MIM | MIM has mature feedstocks, furnaces, MPIF property data, high yield, and very low unit cost after mold tooling is amortized. Metal VPP removes hard tooling and supports rapid design changes, but retains most MIM downstream operations. Its economic window is therefore low-to-medium volume, high part variety, or geometry that is difficult to mold—not stable high-volume production. | (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032) |
| Key patent constraints | Relevant families include Steege/Trio Labs’ in-situ powder/resin infusion and projected-light powder-composite fabrication, priority 2016 and granted as EP3419802B1; Opschoor/ECN–Admatec’s metal-precursor slurry, conversion, debinding, and sintering route, priority 2015 and published as WO2017081160A1; and Caltech’s photopolymerized or infused metal-salt hydrogel routes. Claim scope, territorial status, ownership, and freedom to operate require patent-counsel review. | (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037) |


*Table: Key technical, qualification, intellectual-property, and competitive barriers governing the commercial viability of sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization.*

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym

        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. How commercially viable is sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization?
1. Who has commercialized it (printer vendors, feedstock suppliers, parts services), with founding
   dates, funding, ownership changes and failures (for example Holo's 2024 asset sale to Greene Group,
   and Nano Dimension's 2022 purchase and 2025 exit of Admatec), and installed base where reported.
2. Which markets and applications have actually adopted it, with named examples: orthodontic and
   dental parts, medical and surgical instruments, watch and jewelry parts, micromechanics, RF and
   microwave parts, copper cold plates and heat sinks for electronics, electrical interconnects,
   nozzles and fluidics, tooling inserts, and any defense or aerospace use.
3. Economics: printer price, feedstock cost, build rate, parts per build, cost per part against MIM
   (break-even volume once mold tooling is counted), binder jetting and micro laser powder bed fusion,
   and typical lead times.
4. Barriers: part size and wall-thickness limits, feedstock availability, qualification and standards
   (MPIF Standard 35, ISO/ASTM 52900 classification), the key patents and who holds them, and
   competition.
5. Your judgement of where the process is headed and which niches it can hold.
Cite peer-reviewed papers, standards, market reports and trade press, and flag any figure that comes
only from a vendor.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to answer this multi-faceted question about sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization's commercial viability.

Abstract:
Copper’s high thermal and electrical conductivity enables its application in heat exchangers and high-frequency components. For those applications, additive manufacturing has advantages with respect to functional integration, miniaturization, and reduced waste. However, the processing of copper is a challenge for established laser-based processes since copper’s high reflectivity impedes energy input. Sinter-based additive manufacturing processes do not exhibit this limitation since the energy for the fusion of material is applied by thermal energy during sintering. This makes them an ideal candidate for copper manufacturing. In the following work, Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing (LMM) of copper is demonstrated. Curing behavior is investigated by single-layer exposure (SLE) tests measuring curing thickness for different loading factors, particle sizes, and exposure times. Bending strength is investigated as a function of exposure time, loading factor, and orientation in the building space. A higher exposure time and lower loading factors increase bending strength. Furthermore, samples with different loading factors are produced to measure the impact of the loading factor on sintered density. For these parameters, no clear trend is demonstrated.

Abstract:
Aluminum nitride (AlN) is an excellent material for heat sinks and is used, for example, in high-performance electronics, high-power LEDs and photovoltaics. In order to meet the constantly increasing demands on substrate materials and heat sinks resulting from the permanent increase in power density and resulting heat in electronic components, new types of components made of high-performance materials with highly complex geometries are required. In this work, AlN based on a commercial powder (“TOYALNITE®”-JCGA-BLY5 by Toyal Europe), was successfully qualified for an AM technology through suspension and process development for CerAM VPP—a DLP-based vat photo polymerization technology. The properties of the components were characterized along the entire process chain, achieving densities of 3.33 g/cm3 (>99% Th.D.) and excellent thermal conductivities of more than 180 W/mK, which are comparable to state-of-the-art for conventionally manufactured AlN components. Homogeneous microstructures of good quality confirm the measured density and thermal conductivity. A complex-shaped component usable for an exemplary heating–cooling application demonstrates the potential of this development.

Abstract:
Functionally Graded Materials (FGMs) offer discrete or continuously changing properties/compositions over the volume of the parts. The widespread application of FGMs was not rapid enough in the past due to limitations of the manufacturing methods. Significant developments in manufacturing technologies especially in Additive Manufacturing (AM) enable us nowadays to manufacture materials with specified changes over the volume/surface of components. The use of AM methods for the manufacturing of FGMs may allow us to compensate for some drawbacks of conventional methods and to produce complex and near-net-shaped structures with better control of gradients in a cost-efficient way. Vat Photopolymerization (VP), a type of AM method that works according to the principle of curing liquid photopolymer resin layer-by-layer, has gained in recent years high importance due to its advantages such as low cost, high surface quality control, no need to support structures, no limitation in the material. This article reviews the state-of-art and future potential of using VP methods for FGM manufacturing. It was concluded that improvements in printer hardware setup and software, design aspects and printing methodologies will accelerate the use of VP methods for FGMs manufacturing.
