   Five overlays complete the route record. First, exposure architecture distinguishes scanned, projected, masked, continuous,
tomographic and highly localised routes without promoting every implementation to a separate category. Continuous liquid-
interface production changes the exposure-transport boundary but retains formulation, conversion and final-property controls [10].
Second, this review uses three explicit route conventions. In a direct route, the printed object supplies the material of the delivered
part, although conditioning may remain. In an indirect route, the printed object is a green preform, pattern, mould, core or
sacrificial tool that is materially transformed, consumed or removed. In an integrated hybrid route, additive and non-additive
operations alternate inside one controlled chain, for example deposition interleaved with measurement and machining. This differs
from an external comparator such as a wholly machined or moulded route. Third, every candidate needs a state-transformation
record. Fourth, a functional-material overlay is required for conductive, ESD, dielectric, magnetic, optical, radiation-functional,
adaptive and soft systems because shape fidelity does not establish service function. Fifth, adjacent solid-state metal-deposition
routes are recorded by their mechanism and delivered state even when an exact placement in the seven-category taxonomy is not
asserted.

3. The feedstock-to-delivered-part chain
   Figure 1 defines the minimum object-state chain. "As printed" is a final state only when no mandatory transformation remains
and acceptance evidence is valid in that state.

   Polymer material extrusion can produce the final polymer chemistry directly, yet bead orientation and interlayer formation
remain part of the material state. Ahn et  al. demonstrated direction- and process-variable dependence in one acrylonitrile-
butadiene-styrene system; that result establishes an anisotropy gate, not a transferable percentage [8]. Polymer PBF may avoid
separate supports for many geometries, but powder history and thermal exposure remain consequential. Vendittoli et al. reported
changes in reused polyamide 12 powder and parts within their selective-laser-sintering workflow, supporting lot-history and
refresh-policy controls without defining a universal reuse limit [9].
   Photopolymerisation transfers another set of variables. Cured geometry depends on absorption, scattering, exposure, separation
and transport, while the delivered network depends on washing, post-cure and conditioning. Filled photopolymers intensify the
coupling: particles alter viscosity, sedimentation, scattering and cure depth, while the binder must either remain as a composite
phase or be removed without damaging a green body.
   In metal and ceramic sinter-based routes, the printer intentionally creates an intermediate. Bound-metal extrusion, binder jetting
and LMM all require a green-to-final transformation, but their green structures arise by different mechanisms. Shima et al. linked
deposition and densification to microstructure and tensile behaviour in a specific 17-4PH bound-metal workflow [14]. Chen et al.
and Cabo Rios et al. showed that binder-jet printing conditions and sintering can control densification and directional dimensional
evolution in 316L systems [15,16]. LMM studies likewise separate suspension preparation and cure from debinding and sintering
[17,18]. Final-metal properties therefore cannot be assigned to the printed green state, and nominally identical furnace schedules
are not presumed transferable across green-body architectures.

deposition deformation and the fired ceramic outcome in one boehmite-derived alumina system [22]. The transferable logic is

causal: the ink must flow through the nozzle, recover sufficient structure, dry without unacceptable damage and survive thermal
conversion. The study's numerical criteria remain specific to that ink and test configuration.
   Glass-forming routes impose a similar boundary. Kotz et al. demonstrated that a photocurable nanocomposite can be shaped
and thermally converted into fused-silica structures [23]. That evidence supports a multistage route, not the claim that any silica-
filled resin will become transparent glass. Particle identity, loading, dispersion, organic removal, shrinkage, bubbles and thermal
history belong to the delivered optical material.
   Reinforced and soft systems show different transition risks. Matsuzaki et al. used in-nozzle impregnation to print continuous-
fibre composites, making reinforcement path and interface formation explicit variables [24]. Hinton et al. used a reversible support
bath to stabilise complex hydrogel geometries [25]. In each case, the environment surrounding deposition is part of the route;
demonstration of shape retention is not long-term mechanical, biological or service qualification.

5. Conditional advantages and process-specific losses
  An advantage should be assigned to one of three levels. A mechanistic advantage follows from the shaping principle. A
demonstrated advantage requires matched evidence for the material, machine, geometry and workflow. A factory advantage
requires accepted-part throughput, labour, yield and cell-cost evidence. Without a comparator and boundary, the statement remains
an unresolved claim.
5.1 Polymer-dominant routes
   Material extrusion can place material selectively with comparatively simple feedstock handling and can scale from fine
filament deposition to high-flow pellet systems. Its mechanistic losses include bead-scale surface texture, direction-dependent
interfaces, start/stop defects, thermal gradients and support-access constraints. Larger nozzles may improve volumetric deposition
while sacrificing feature access and surface state; smaller nozzles reverse that trade-off.
   Polymer PBF uses surrounding powder as geometric support for many features and permits three-dimensional batch nesting.

5.1 Polymer-dominant routes
   Material extrusion can place material selectively with comparatively simple feedstock handling and can scale from fine
filament deposition to high-flow pellet systems. Its mechanistic losses include bead-scale surface texture, direction-dependent
interfaces, start/stop defects, thermal gradients and support-access constraints. Larger nozzles may improve volumetric deposition
while sacrificing feature access and surface state; smaller nozzles reverse that trade-off.
   Polymer PBF uses surrounding powder as geometric support for many features and permits three-dimensional batch nesting.
The complete cycle includes bed preparation, heating, building, cooling, excavation, depowdering, powder segregation or refresh
and surface finishing. Internal channels can be geometrically printable yet operationally unacceptable if powder cannot be removed
or verified.
  VPP can localise cure through scanning, projection or masking and can provide fine exposure-defined features. Its losses
include support contact, separation forces, residual liquid, washing, post-cure, oxygen or optical effects and conversion gradients.
Continuous exposure can alter vertical transport and machine occupancy [10], but speed remains geometry-, resin- and acceptance-
dependent. Material jetting offers spatial placement and multimaterial potential, yet the result depends on droplet formation,
temperature, rheology, waveform, nozzle condition and support strategy. Chen et al. demonstrated that coupling in one waveform-
modelled material-jetting system [11]; its operating window is not a generic printhead or ink specification.
5.2 Fusion, sinter-based and solid-state metal routes
   Laser PBF (L-PBF) can create complex metal geometries through local melting, but  it combines powder handling, rapid
thermal  cycling, support  design,  residual  stress, surface roughness and  internal-defect  control.  Ultrafast X-ray work by
Cunningham et  al. linked pore formation to a keyhole-regime transition in a bounded laser-melting experiment [12]. The
transferable lesson is that nominal energy density does not replace control of the melt regime. Electron-beam PBF (EB-PBF)
changes the energy source, vacuum environment and preheat strategy; Al-Bermani et al. linked thermal history to microstructural
diversity and properties in Ti-6Al-4V [13].
  DED and WAAM can add material to existing components, repair local regions and generate large near-net forms. Their
conditional benefit is deposition access and material addition where fine powder-bed feature control may not be the objective.
Their losses include high heat input, thermal accumulation, residual stress, deformation, coarse surface state and machining
allowance. Carroll et al. reported directional tensile behaviour in DED Ti-6Al-4V [26], while Ma et al. treated scanning strategy as
a control variable for stress and deformation in one WAAM Al-Si system [27].
   Binder jetting, bound-metal extrusion and LMM move much of the consolidation burden from the printer to debinding and
sintering. This can reduce melt-related thermal stress during shaping and enable batch furnace processing, but it creates a fragile
intermediate,  dimensional  transformation,  furnace  loading  constraints and  risks from  binder  removal,  atmosphere and
contamination. Binder jetting adds green-part excavation; bound extrusion adds bead interfaces and green anisotropy; LMM
couples metal loading to suspension flow and optical cure. Output must be measured after sintering and final acceptance.
    Solid-state metal deposition changes the governing invalidation gates because consolidation proceeds without intentional bulk
melting. In cold-spray AM, powder morphology and native particle state interact with particle flight, impact conditions, bonding
and deposited properties. Anumandla et al. demonstrated those couplings for commercially pure titanium powders of different
manufacture and morphology [34]. A candidate route therefore needs controls for powder identity, particle-size and shape
distributions, gas and nozzle conditions, substrate preparation, interparticle and substrate bonding, deposited defects and any
finishing required; absence of melting does not itself prove an acceptable interface or property state.
  AFSD uses thermomechanical deformation and plastic flow rather than local melting and solidification. Kincaid et  al.
combined AFSD with structured-light measurement, turning and milling in two manufacturing demonstrations [35]. Their work
shows why a near-net deposit that requires measurement and machining is an integrated hybrid chain: coordinate transfer, datum
strategy, deposition allowance, tool access and operation sequence contribute directly to the accepted geometry. Cold spray and

AFSD are retained here as adjacent solid-state metal-deposition routes and are not forced into an unverified exact position within
the seven-category taxonomy.
   Sheet lamination occupies another solid-state boundary. UAM bonds metal foils at relatively low bulk temperature and can
embed temperature-sensitive elements. Hehr et al. demonstrated integration of fibre-optic strain sensors within metal using UAM
[28]. This establishes an opportunity under the studied conditions, not general production qualification; interface, foil, geometry,
machining and sensor-survival evidence remain necessary.
5.3 Advanced and highly specialised materials
   Nano/micron feedstocks should be classified by physical form, chemistry, surface state, dispersion route and whether the
particulate phase remains in the component. A nanopowder, agglomerate, nanofibre, micronised powder, concentrate and ready-to-
print resin are not interchangeable. For a retained composite, particle distribution, interface state, orientation and percolation may
control function. For an indirect metal, ceramic or glass route, the carrier must be removed and the particles consolidated; final
function belongs to the transformed structure, not the wet formulation.
   Highly specialised resins should be selected from service state backward. Electrical or ESD materials require geometry-specific
resistance and contact evidence. Thermally conductive systems require direction, interface and boundary-condition control.
Dielectric, ferroelectric, piezoelectric and magnetic systems may require alignment, poling or field-history records. Optical,
photonic, luminescent and radiation-functional systems require spectral, attenuation, dose or energy definitions. Extreme-service
resins require the actual temperature, chemical, flame, barrier or insulation test. Adaptive and soft systems require activation,
recovery, fatigue, solvent or humidity state. These topics are assigned to ER-156-ER-161; ER-139 defines their common selection
boundary.

evaluated separately from material storage, atmosphere, recovery, cleaning, curing, furnaces, machining, ventilation, waste
handling, metrology, maintenance and operator competence.

   Safety evidence must be bounded by task and facility. In a 2025 National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
evaluation of one metal-powder AM facility, airborne particles increased during tasks, metals were detected in breathing zones and
on surfaces, skin and clothing, and feedstock powder migrated through production and non-production areas; measured breathing-
zone values were below the applicable occupational exposure limits in that facility [29]. This facility-specific result shows why
powder transfer, depowdering, cleaning, maintenance and transport belong in the process map; it does not establish another site's
exposure or compliance.
   For desktop VPP, NIOSH identifies uncured resin, acrylates, cleaning solvents, curing emissions and sanding dust as exposure-
control topics and recommends appropriate ventilation, handling and personal protection [30]. Nano/micron materials require
separate hazard and exposure assessment based on composition and physical form. Current NIOSH nanotechnology guidance
directs users to containment, engineering-control, sampling and material-specific resources rather than treating "nano" as one
hazard class [31]. Particle size alone neither proves nor excludes risk.

7. Economics without marketing shortcuts
   The primary production denominator is accepted output from the complete cell:


                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139 · 2026 · Page 5                                                                                                                 3Dresyns Engineering Publications · ER-139


 Effective cell throughput = accepted components delivered / observation period, measured at steady state for the declared batch
                                            mix and utilisation.
   Lead time is separate: it is the elapsed time from released feedstock to final acceptance for one batch. In a pipelined cell,
steady-state throughput is controlled by the bottleneck stage rather than by the sum of one batch's stage times. Printer output, lead
time and cell throughput must therefore be reported independently.
   The  cost boundary  includes equipment occupancy,  labour,  feedstock  loss,  reusable  fractions, consumables,  utilities,
atmosphere, supports, cleaning, post-processing, inspection, maintenance, rework, scrap and failed qualification. A route may have
low marginal geometry cost but high recovery labour; high printer output but a furnace bottleneck; good material utilisation but
costly containment; or rapid green-part output followed by low final yield.
   Comparisons should freeze annual volume, part mix, geometry, acceptance criteria, utilisation, queue model and comparator.
Machining, moulding, casting and a separately defined integrated hybrid chain are legitimate comparators when they deliver the
same accepted state. AM should not receive credit for unused geometric freedom or customisation, and the comparator should not
be burdened with tooling or inventory assumptions absent from the actual case.
   Environmental claims require the same boundary discipline. "Less waste" may describe near-net placement while omitting
supports, unrecoverable powder, solvents, inert gas, furnaces, failed parts or machining. This framework retains energy and
material flow as case variables but assigns no universal sustainability rank.

8. Qualification architecture and change control
  ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 separates industrial-process and production-site requirements from the claim that a particular part is
qualified [2]. ISO/ASTM 52927:2024 maps main AM characteristics to corresponding test methods, while ISO/ASTM 52928:2024
addresses metal-powder life-cycle management [3,4]. These standards help structure controlled records; they do not replace
application-specific acceptance criteria.
  A minimum qualification architecture contains:
 1. Feedstock record: identity, supplier or preparation route, lot, storage, age, conditioning, reuse or blending history, and process-
     controlling properties.
 2. Machine-state record: configuration, software and parameter set, calibration, maintenance, critical consumables, atmosphere and
     pre-build checks.
 3. Build record: geometry revision, scale check, orientation, nesting, supports, exposure or deposition history, interruptions and in-
     process evidence.
 4. Transition record: recovery, washing, cure, drying, debinding, sintering, infiltration, heat treatment, machining, polishing and
     conditioning, including equipment identity and load configuration.
 5. Measurement record: traceable dimensional, surface,  internal-defect, composition, microstructure, mechanical or functional
     evidence with uncertainty appropriate to the decision.
 6. Acceptance record: intended use, critical characteristics, direct-inspection or validated indirect-verification strategy, sampling logic,
    non-conformance disposition and linkage between specimens and production parts.
 7. Change-control record: rules for reassessing material, machine, geometry, parameters, post-process equipment, site, software or
     inspection changes.
   NIST's part-qualification programme highlights measurement challenges created by complex surfaces and internal geometry,
defects, anisotropy, residual stress and post-processing [7]. Those challenges make "same material and printer" an inadequate
equivalence argument. Qualification should follow the causal route from feedstock and machine state to the features that control
final performance.

P Mastny. High-strength copper alloys for indirect additive manufacturing using photolithography. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt provides only partial specifications for the Incus Hammer Lab35 and does not describe Admaflex printers. The Hammer Lab35 is identified as Incus GmbH’s first commercial lithography-based metal manufacturing (LMM) printer. Its feedstock is a solid block at ambient temperature, consisting of metal powder suspended in a photocurable organic binder; the printer chamber is cooled to keep this feedstock solid. Feedstock is delivered by a heated blade that forms a smooth layer and a feedstock roller, with viscosity and powder particle size affecting print quality and achievable layer height. EP3419802B1 concerns Trio Labs inventor Adam T. C. Steege’s method and apparatus for solid freeform fabrication—additive manufacturing of metal, plastic, ceramic, and composite objects—using an “in situ infusion” approach. The excerpt explains the general context: a digital model is divided into horizontal slices, and successive two-dimensional layers are formed on a build surface. It discusses powder-based processes in which a binder or adhesive joins particles, followed by post-processing such as binder removal and thermal sintering; this can produce a “brown” part that shrinks as voids are eliminated and may reach near-full density. The cited prior-art example uses a photocurable adhesive sprayed onto powder, selectively cured with planar light, and repeated layer by layer. The patent’s apparent innovation is therefore a different or improved integration of material infusion and photopolymerization during powder-composite fabrication, intended to create more accurate, functional parts from powder materials. However, the supplied excerpt ends at the beginning of the invention summary and does not disclose the specific in-situ infusion sequence, apparatus, photopolymer chemistry, powder composition, or detailed mechanism for fabricating metal parts. ## pqac-00000036

From text 'saccone2022microscalefabricationof pages 9-12'.

Max Saccone, Rebecca A. Gallivan, Kai Narita, Daryl W. Yee, and Julia R. Greer. Microscale fabrication of 3d multicomponent metals via hydrogel infusion. Unknown journal, May 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-1108933/v1, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-1108933/v1.

The excerpt does not identify or describe the Steege/Trio Labs/Holo patent EP3419802B1 specifically, so it cannot establish the patent’s claims, inventors, or exact scope. It does, however, describe a closely related hydrogel-infusion additive-manufacturing concept (HIAM). Its central innovation is separating part formation from inorganic-material selection: a single photoresin is optimized for vat photopolymerization, the polymer scaffold is shaped first, and water-soluble metal precursors are infused afterward. This avoids designing a separate particle-loaded slurry or hybrid resin for every composition and enables compositional flexibility, including refractory metals, high-entropy alloys, and multimaterial structures. For metal fabrication, the infused metal salts occupy the hydrogel/polymer network, are converted during thermal treatment into metal oxides, and are subsequently reduced with hydrogen gas to form metals or alloys. messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Barrier | Description | Evidence source |
|---|---|---|
| Part size and wall thickness | The process is best suited to small, intricate parts. Thick or closed sections lengthen binder-transport paths and raise cracking, residue, distortion, and inspection risks. Minimum printable walls also differ from minimum cleanable gaps or channels; projector pixel pitch is not final-part resolution. Published limits are machine-, alloy-, orientation-, and geometry-specific rather than universal. | Segurola identifies small intricate components as the opportunity and thick or closed regions as the controlling liability; it requires final-state feature mapping rather than reliance on pixel pitch. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007) |
| Cure–loading trade-off | Higher metal loading reduces binder content and sintering distance but increases viscosity, agglomeration, settling, and optical attenuation. Lower loading improves flow and cure depth but increases organic-removal burden and shrinkage. Copper experiments show cure thickness and green strength depend jointly on loading, particle size, exposure, and orientation. | Segurola’s review synthesizes the coupled optical–rheological trade-off and cites Scheibler et al.’s 2024 copper study. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009) |
| Feedstock availability and alloy transferability | A powder qualified for MIM, LPBF, binder jetting, or extrusion is not automatically suitable for metal VPP: surface chemistry, oxide state, particle size, dispersion, optical response, and rheology all matter. Commercial feedstocks cover only a limited set of qualified alloys, and each powder–binder–printer–furnace combination needs validation. Incus literature documents successful 316L and copper processing, not universal metal compatibility. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000033) |
| Cleaning and debinding | Surrounding uncured feedstock must be removed from surfaces and internal passages without eroding fragile green features. Blind, narrow, or tortuous channels may print successfully yet fail cleaning. During debinding, gas evolution and long transport paths can cause cracks, blisters, delamination, residue, or chemistry changes; the brown body may be weaker than the green body. | Incus processing involves decaking, solvent cleaning, solvent debinding, thermal debinding, and sintering; Segurola treats cleanability and geometry-specific debinding as separate qualification gates. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000043) |
| Shrinkage and dimensional control | Shrinkage is anisotropic and geometry-, orientation-, packing-, furnace-load-, and setter-dependent. A single isotropic scale factor cannot reliably compensate walls, holes, lattices, and massive sections. Setters reduce sag but can constrain contraction, mark surfaces, or introduce contamination. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008) |
| Reactive and precipitation-strengthened alloys | Alloys optimized for fusion AM may sinter poorly. For example, Cr₂Nb strengthens GRCop-42 but pins boundaries and inhibits pressureless densification; Cr/Nb oxides and trace water in hydrogen can impair wetting and disrupt phases. This is directly relevant to Cu–Cr–Zr, Cu–Cr–Nb, Al–Zr, and similar oxide-sensitive development programs. | Mastny’s GRCop-42 study found pressureless solid-state sintering impractical without additional liquid-phase strategies and documented oxide and wetting sensitivity. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |
| Qualification and standards | ISO/ASTM 52900 classifies the shaping step as vat photopolymerization, but the delivered product is a sintered metal part. Applicable frameworks include ISO/ASTM 52901, 52907, 52920, 52927, 52931, 52951, and 52953. These organize purchasing, powder characterization, site qualification, testing, safety, and data—not alloy-specific acceptance. MPIF Standard 35 remains a useful MIM/property comparator, but it does not qualify an LMM process or its dimensional capability. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009) |
| Competition from binder jetting | Binder jetting generally offers larger build envelopes, three-dimensional nesting, broader industrial powder ecosystems, and high green-part throughput. Its disadvantages are depowdering, lower green strength, binder-placement resolution, and the same furnace and shrinkage burden. Metal VPP competes where finer surfaces and smaller features justify lower scale and more difficult slurry handling. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031) |
| Competition from micro-LPBF | Micro-LPBF directly consolidates metal and avoids cleaning uncured resin plus debinding, but carries melt-pool, support, residual-stress, reflectivity, thermal-distortion, powder-safety, and surface-roughness burdens. Metal VPP is attractive for reflective copper and fine, smooth batches, but only if sintering preserves chemistry, density, and dimensions. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000031) |
| Competition from MIM | MIM has mature feedstocks, furnaces, MPIF property data, high yield, and very low unit cost after mold tooling is amortized. Metal VPP removes hard tooling and supports rapid design changes, but retains most MIM downstream operations. Its economic window is therefore low-to-medium volume, high part variety, or geometry that is difficult to mold—not stable high-volume production. | (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032) |

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Commercial Viability of Sinter-Based Metal Vat Photopolymerization

## 1. Commercialization Landscape

Sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization (VPP) is an indirect additive-manufacturing route classified under ISO/ASTM 52900 as vat photopolymerisation. Patterned light selectively cures a photoactive binder loaded with metal powder layer by layer, producing a green composite that is subsequently cleaned, debound, and sintered—a process chain shared with metal injection molding (MIM) (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). The field is served by a small number of printer vendors, feedstock suppliers, and parts services, summarized below.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Incus GmbH** (Vienna, Austria, reported spinoff ~2019 from the Lithoz/TU Wien ecosystem) produces the Hammer Lab35 and Hammer Pro40 printers, which define "Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing" (LMM). The Hammer uses a top-exposure DLP projector above a cooled build platform; feedstock is a solid block of metal powder in a photocurable binder that is spread as a temperature-conditioned paste by a heated blade. The system has interchangeable small, medium, and large platform sizes. After printing, the green part is encased in surrounding feedstock, decaked, cleaned with the water-based solvent Incusol, solvent-debound, thermally debound, and sintered under reducing atmosphere (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000043). Incus has demonstrated 316L stainless steel and copper through to sintered components, and its promotional materials list 17-4PH, tool steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, and precious metals; peer-reviewed academic studies independently confirm 316L and Cu processing (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012). Installed base figures were not independently verified in the retrieved literature.

**Holo Inc.** (California, founded 2017; underlying patent priority 2016 from inventor Adam Steege at Trio Labs, Research Triangle Park, NC) developed the PureForm platform, a film-fed bottom-up DLP system for production of metal parts. The European patent EP 3 419 802 B1 (proprietor: Trio Labs, Inc.) covers a method and apparatus for solid freeform fabrication using particulate material combined with photocurable resin, planar DLP or raster exposure, debinding, and sintering (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000035). Holo reported pure copper parts exceeding 92% IACS conductivity, followed by 17-4PH and 316L stainless steels (vendor-reported figures). The company raised venture funding but did not establish a broad printer-sales business. **Greene Group Industries** (a US MIM contract manufacturer based in Connecticut) **acquired Holo's assets in March 2024** and now offers a parts service in 17-4PH and 316L, with a published design guide specifying 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm maximum wall, ±0.025 mm tolerance up to 12 mm, and 0.8–1.6 μm Ra as printed (vendor-reported). Holo's trajectory—from venture-backed startup to asset sale—constitutes a partial commercial failure of the standalone-printer business model, although the process survives as a contract service.

**Admatec Europe B.V.** (Alkmaar, Netherlands, reported founding ~2013) manufactures the Admaflex 130 and Admaflex 300 DLP printers, which use a tape-casting or slurry-delivery recoating mechanism (pqac-00000026). The company has a stronger commercial footprint in ceramic VPP (alumina, zirconia) than in metal VPP, though a related patent (WO 2017 081 160 A1, priority 2015, inventor Jan Opschoor, originally assigned to ECN) covers a radiation-curable slurry containing 55–98 wt% metal-precursor particles, photopolymerisation, debinding, precursor conversion, and sintering—an approach designed to improve optical penetration by using metal-oxide or metal-salt precursors whose refractive index better matches the resin (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041). **Nano Dimension acquired Admatec in 2022 and announced an exit/divestment in 2025**, a negative signal for standalone metal-DLP scale-up.

**Lithoz GmbH** (Vienna, founded 2011, TU Wien spinoff) is the parent-technology benchmark for lithography-based ceramic manufacturing (LCM) using CeraFab printers, from which Incus's metal-adapted technology emerged (pqac-00000012). Lithoz itself is not a principal metal-VPP supplier but its suspension-handling, debinding, and sintering knowledge base is foundational.

**3Dresyns / Resyner Technologies S.L.** (Donostia–San Sebastián, Spain) supplies open-material photopolymer binders, dispersants, and LMM feedstock formulations intended for user validation on SLA/DLP hardware, offering water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009).

## 2. Markets and Applications

Peer-reviewed evidence identifies several application domains, though independently verified production deployments at named end-users remain scarce.

**Copper thermal and electrical components.** Copper's high reflectivity makes it challenging for laser-based PBF, giving sinter-based VPP a mechanistic advantage. Scheibler et al. (2024) demonstrated LMM of copper on the Incus Hammer, characterising cure depth and green strength as functions of loading, particle size, and exposure (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Roumanie et al. (2021) linked debinding and sintering conditions to copper composition and thermal conductivity in a highly loaded photocurable route (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). Target applications include micro heat exchangers, high-frequency components, cold plates, and electrical interconnects (pqac-00000012). Holo's copper-conductivity claims (>92% IACS) were directed at electronics thermal management, though these remain vendor-reported.

**Shape-memory and advanced alloys.** Cohen et al. (2023) demonstrated sinter-based LMM of NiTi shape-memory alloy and identified carbon/phase sensitivity in the process (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). This is relevant to medical devices and aerospace actuators, but the carbon sensitivity highlights that binder chemistry directly affects functional properties.

**Micro-architected metals and metamaterials.** Melentiev et al. (2024) demonstrated high-resolution 316L complex structures with fine features, hollow architectures, and measured surface/property data using DLP (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The same group separately examined thin-walled 316L metamaterial debinding/sintering relationships (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). **Where the process is unlikely to compete:**
- High-volume production (>~5,000–10,000 identical parts), where MIM's amortised tooling cost dominates.
- Large parts (typically >~50 mm), where binder jetting and LPBF offer vastly larger build envelopes.
- Alloys requiring very tight chemistry control (e.g., Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr) where binder-derived carbon and oxygen contamination is unacceptable and sintering science is immature.
- Precipitation-hardened copper alloys (Cu-Cr-Zr, GRCop-42) where pressureless sintering is fundamentally impeded by dispersoid-pinned grain boundaries and oxide sensitivity (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014).

**For a university alloy-development lab** with Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, and Cu-Cr-Zr interests and its own ultrasonic atomisation capability, sinter-based metal VPP is currently most relevant as a copper and stainless-steel shaping route. Extending it to aluminium alloys or precipitation-strengthened copper alloys would require fundamental sintering research beyond the current state of the art. The lab's ultrasonic atomisation of fine powder (D50 < 20 μm) is well suited to the particle-size requirements of LMM feedstocks, but powder surface chemistry, oxide state, and compatibility with photocurable binders would need to be established experimentally for each alloy system."}

# Commercial Viability of Sinter-Based Metal Vat Photopolymerization

## 1. Commercialization Landscape

Sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization (VPP) is an indirect additive-manufacturing route classified under ISO/ASTM 52900 as vat photopolymerisation. Patterned light selectively cures a photoactive binder loaded with metal powder layer by layer, producing a green composite that is subsequently cleaned, debound, and sintered—a process chain shared with metal injection molding (MIM) (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 2-3). The field is served by a small number of printer vendors, feedstock suppliers, and parts services, summarized below.

| Company | Headquarters | Founded / spinoff date | Technology / printer model | Exposure architecture | Key materials demonstrated | Ownership / funding events | Current status |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Incus GmbH** | Vienna, Austria | **2019**; reported spinoff from Lithoz/TU Wien | **Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing (LMM); Hammer Lab35 / Hammer Pro40** | Top-exposure DLP onto temperature-conditioned, paste-like feedstock spread by a heated blade; removable material surrounds the green part. The academic description confirms interchangeable platform sizes and a DLP projector above the build plane. (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloysa pages 9-11) | Commercially promoted: 316L, 17-4PH, tool steels, Ti-6Al-4V, Cu, precious metals; peer-reviewed or academic demonstrations include 316L and Cu. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11) | Originated from Lithoz-associated technology; funding history and installed-base totals were not verified in the retrieved primary sources. | Active printer, feedstock and process supplier. The Hammer platform is the best-published surviving dedicated metal-LMM system, but reported specifications and installed base remain substantially vendor-controlled. |
| **Holo Inc. / Trio Labs / Greene Group Industries** | Holo: California, US; Trio Labs: North Carolina, US; Greene Group: Connecticut, US | Holo **2017**; Steege patent priority **2016** | **PureForm** parts-production platform; underlying Steege/Trio Labs powder-composite patent family | Film-fed, bottom-up projected-light process reported for PureForm. The Steege patent covers particulate-plus-photocurable-resin composite layers, planar DLP or raster exposure, debinding and sintering; the European patent lists Trio Labs as proprietor. (EP3419802B1 pages 1-3, EP3419802B1 pages 3-4) | Pure Cu reported above **92% IACS**, followed by 17-4PH and 316L stainless steels; figures are company-reported unless independently qualified. | Holo raised venture funding but did not establish a broad printer-sales business; **Greene Group Industries acquired Holo’s assets in March 2024** and continued the process as a parts service. | Holo no longer operates as the original independent venture; commercialization survives principally through Greene Group’s contract-manufacturing service. Separately, Pires *et al.* compared supplied micro-DLP 316L with binder-jetted and laser-melted 316L, but proprietary process details and unmatched specimen scales limit route-wide conclusions. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11) |
| **Admatec Europe B.V.** | Alkmaar, Netherlands | **2013** (reported) | **Admaflex 130 / Admaflex 300** | DLP with tape-casting or slurry-recoating material delivery; Admaflex 130 is independently documented as a commercial DLP system. (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7) | Primarily alumina, zirconia, silica and other ceramics; metal demonstrations or offerings have included 316L, Cu and metal-precursor routes. The Opschoor patent covers 55–98 wt% metal-precursor slurry, photopolymerization, debinding, precursor conversion and sintering. (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7, WO2017081160A1 pages 15-17) | **Nano Dimension acquired Admatec in 2022**; Nano Dimension announced or executed an **exit/divestment in 2025**. | Commercial legacy is much stronger in ceramic VPP than production metal VPP. The ownership reversal is a negative signal for standalone metal-DLP scale-up, although installed machines and process IP remain relevant. |
| **Lithoz GmbH** | Vienna, Austria | **2011**; TU Wien spinoff | **Lithography-based Ceramic Manufacturing; CeraFab family** | Bottom-up DLP/LCM using highly filled photocurable suspensions | Commercial focus is ceramics rather than metals; its importance here is the machine, suspension, recoating, debinding and sintering knowledge base from which Incus emerged. | Privately held; associated with the technological lineage that produced Incus. | Active and commercially established in ceramic VPP, but not itself a principal supplier of sinter-based metal-VPP systems. Included as the parent-technology benchmark rather than a direct metal competitor. |
| **3Dresyns / Resyner Technologies S.L.** | Donostia–San Sebastián, Spain | Not verified in retrieved sources | Open-material photopolymer resins, binders, dispersants and user-formulated **LMM feedstocks** rather than a dedicated metal printer | Intended for SLA/DLP systems using powder-filled reactive binders; offers water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families, with validation assigned to the user. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 5-6, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11) | Supplier claims broad compatibility with metal and metal-precursor powders; no single alloy/process window should be inferred without powder–binder–printer–furnace qualification. | No major acquisition or institutional-funding event verified in the retrieved evidence. | Active specialist feedstock supplier. Useful for research and open-material development, but not equivalent to a turnkey, qualified production ecosystem. |


*Table: Key printer, feedstock and parts-service participants, including ownership changes and the distinction between independently documented capabilities and vendor-reported claims. Dates and transactions not supported by the retrieved technical literature are identified as reported rather than independently verified.*

**Incus GmbH** (Vienna, Austria, reported spinoff ~2019 from the Lithoz/TU Wien ecosystem) produces the Hammer Lab35 and Hammer Pro40 printers, which define "Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing" (LMM). The Hammer uses a top-exposure DLP projector above a cooled build platform; feedstock is a solid block of metal powder in a photocurable binder that is spread as a temperature-conditioned paste by a heated blade. The system has interchangeable small, medium, and large platform sizes. After printing, the green part is encased in surrounding feedstock, decaked, cleaned with the water-based solvent Incusol, solvent-debound, thermally debound, and sintered under reducing atmosphere (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloysa pages 9-11, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys media 2245fb35). Incus has demonstrated 316L stainless steel and copper through to sintered components, and its promotional materials list 17-4PH, tool steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, and precious metals; peer-reviewed academic studies independently confirm 316L and Cu processing (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11). Installed base figures were not independently verified in the retrieved literature.

**Holo Inc.** (California, founded 2017; underlying patent priority 2016 from inventor Adam Steege at Trio Labs, Research Triangle Park, NC) developed the PureForm platform, a film-fed bottom-up DLP system for production of metal parts. The European patent EP 3 419 802 B1 (proprietor: Trio Labs, Inc.) covers a method and apparatus for solid freeform fabrication using particulate material combined with photocurable resin, planar DLP or raster exposure, debinding, and sintering (EP3419802B1 pages 1-3, EP3419802B1 pages 3-4). Holo reported pure copper parts exceeding 92% IACS conductivity, followed by 17-4PH and 316L stainless steels (vendor-reported figures). The company raised venture funding but did not establish a broad printer-sales business. **Greene Group Industries** (a US MIM contract manufacturer based in Connecticut) **acquired Holo's assets in March 2024** and now offers a parts service in 17-4PH and 316L, with a published design guide specifying 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm maximum wall, ±0.025 mm tolerance up to 12 mm, and 0.8–1.6 μm Ra as printed (vendor-reported). Holo's trajectory—from venture-backed startup to asset sale—constitutes a partial commercial failure of the standalone-printer business model, although the process survives as a contract service.

**Admatec Europe B.V.** (Alkmaar, Netherlands, reported founding ~2013) manufactures the Admaflex 130 and Admaflex 300 DLP printers, which use a tape-casting or slurry-delivery recoating mechanism (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4). The company has a stronger commercial footprint in ceramic VPP (alumina, zirconia) than in metal VPP, though a related patent (WO 2017 081 160 A1, priority 2015, inventor Jan Opschoor, originally assigned to ECN) covers a radiation-curable slurry containing 55–98 wt% metal-precursor particles, photopolymerisation, debinding, precursor conversion, and sintering—an approach designed to improve optical penetration by using metal-oxide or metal-salt precursors whose refractive index better matches the resin (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7, WO2017081160A1 pages 15-17). **Nano Dimension acquired Admatec in 2022 and announced an exit/divestment in 2025**, a negative signal for standalone metal-DLP scale-up.

**Lithoz GmbH** (Vienna, founded 2011, TU Wien spinoff) is the parent-technology benchmark for lithography-based ceramic manufacturing (LCM) using CeraFab printers, from which Incus's metal-adapted technology emerged (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11). Lithoz itself is not a principal metal-VPP supplier but its suspension-handling, debinding, and sintering knowledge base is foundational.

**3Dresyns / Resyner Technologies S.L.** (Donostia–San Sebastián, Spain) supplies open-material photopolymer binders, dispersants, and LMM feedstock formulations intended for user validation on SLA/DLP hardware, offering water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 5-6, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11).

## 2. Markets and Applications

Peer-reviewed evidence identifies several application domains, though independently verified production deployments at named end-users remain scarce.

**Copper thermal and electrical components.** Copper's high reflectivity makes it challenging for laser-based PBF, giving sinter-based VPP a mechanistic advantage. Scheibler et al. (2024) demonstrated LMM of copper on the Incus Hammer, characterising cure depth and green strength as functions of loading, particle size, and exposure (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 3-4, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 4-5). Roumanie et al. (2021) linked debinding and sintering conditions to copper composition and thermal conductivity in a highly loaded photocurable route (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11). Target applications include micro heat exchangers, high-frequency components, cold plates, and electrical interconnects (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11). Holo's copper-conductivity claims (>92% IACS) were directed at electronics thermal management, though these remain vendor-reported.

**Shape-memory and advanced alloys.** Cohen et al. (2023) demonstrated sinter-based LMM of NiTi shape-memory alloy and identified carbon/phase sensitivity in the process (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11). This is relevant to medical devices and aerospace actuators, but the carbon sensitivity highlights that binder chemistry directly affects functional properties.

**Micro-architected metals and metamaterials.** Melentiev et al. (2024) demonstrated high-resolution 316L complex structures with fine features, hollow architectures, and measured surface/property data using DLP (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 5-6, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 7-8). The same group separately examined thin-walled 316L metamaterial debinding/sintering relationships (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11). These metamaterial and lattice demonstrations target lightweighting, energy absorption, and RF/microwave applications.

**Aerospace and GRCop alloys.** Mastny (2026) investigated pressureless liquid-phase sintering of GRCop-42 (Cu-4at.%Cr-2at.%Nb) for potential LMM processing, motivated by rocket-engine combustion-chamber applications. The study found that Cr₂Nb's grain-boundary pinning and oxide sensitivity made pressureless sintering impractical without liquid-phase aids (silver or bronze 90/10), and that trace water in hydrogen atmospheres degraded wettability (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 5-9, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 11-14, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 14-17). This result is directly relevant to a lab developing Cu-Cr-Zr complements: precipitation-strengthened copper alloys present fundamental sintering barriers that LMM inherits.

**Watch, jewelry, dental, and micromechanics.** Incus lists precious metals and watch/jewelry components among its application targets (vendor-reported). The parent ceramic-VPP ecosystem (Lithoz) has well-documented dental applications. Metal VPP's fine surface finish and batch capability are suited to orthodontic brackets, watch cases, and small medical instruments, though named commercial deployments were not independently verified in the retrieved literature.

## 3. Economics

Quantitative economic data for metal VPP is largely vendor-proprietary. Segurola (2026) provides the most rigorous framework, defining complete-cell economics rather than printer-level metrics (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 5-7):

- **Effective cell throughput** = accepted components delivered / complete elapsed factory-cell time, measured at steady state.
- **Material efficiency** = mass of accepted parts / mass of released input.
- **Cost per accepted part** includes equipment amortisation, occupancy, consumables (feedstock, solvents, setters, gas), labour, queue time, yield loss, failed qualification, and scrap.

The review explicitly states that "printer capital cost is not complete-cell cost" and that the route requires optical calibration, cleaning equipment, ventilation, solvent/water management, debinding and sintering furnaces, gas supply, setters, metrology, maintenance, and qualified personnel (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9). Whole-field DLP exposure can reduce dependence of exposure time on part count within one image, but nesting, cross-sectional area, layer renewal, separation, cleaning, and furnace capacity still govern throughput. A full plate of thin parts may expose efficiently and overload cleaning or furnace fixturing (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9).

The technology selection framework (ER-139) further notes that comparisons must freeze annual volume, part mix, geometry, acceptance criteria, and comparator; AM should not receive credit for unused geometric freedom, and MIM or machining comparators should not be burdened with tooling assumptions absent from the actual case (segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 5-7).

**Indicative positioning versus competitors** (largely from vendor and trade sources, flagged accordingly):
- *Versus MIM:* Metal VPP eliminates mold tooling (typically $10 k–$100 k+) and supports rapid design iteration, but retains all downstream MIM operations (debinding, sintering, inspection). The break-even volume against MIM is therefore low—typically cited by vendors as hundreds to low thousands of parts, below which mold amortisation makes MIM uneconomic.
- *Versus binder jetting:* Binder jetting offers larger build envelopes, 3D nesting, broader powder ecosystems, and higher green throughput, but with coarser resolution and depowdering requirements. Metal VPP competes where finer surfaces and smaller features justify smaller scale and more difficult feedstock handling (segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 4-5).
- *Versus micro-LPBF:* Micro-LPBF directly consolidates metal, avoiding debinding, but carries melt-pool, support, residual-stress, reflectivity, and surface-roughness burdens. Metal VPP is attractive for reflective metals (copper) and for fine, smooth batch production (segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 4-5).

**Printer pricing** is not published in the peer-reviewed literature. Vendor-reported figures place the Incus Hammer systems in the range typical of industrial ceramic/metal DLP systems (roughly €200 k–€500 k, vendor data); Admaflex 130 systems are reported at a lower entry point. These figures exclude furnaces, cleaning stations, and ancillary infrastructure.

## 4. Barriers

The following table summarises the key technical, qualification, intellectual-property, and competitive barriers governing commercial viability.

| Barrier | Description | Evidence source |
|---|---|---|
| Part size and wall thickness | The process is best suited to small, intricate parts. Thick or closed sections lengthen binder-transport paths and raise cracking, residue, distortion, and inspection risks. Minimum printable walls also differ from minimum cleanable gaps or channels; projector pixel pitch is not final-part resolution. Published limits are machine-, alloy-, orientation-, and geometry-specific rather than universal. | Segurola identifies small intricate components as the opportunity and thick or closed regions as the controlling liability; it requires final-state feature mapping rather than reliance on pixel pitch. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 5-6, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 7-8, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9) |
| Cure–loading trade-off | Higher metal loading reduces binder content and sintering distance but increases viscosity, agglomeration, settling, and optical attenuation. Lower loading improves flow and cure depth but increases organic-removal burden and shrinkage. Copper experiments show cure thickness and green strength depend jointly on loading, particle size, exposure, and orientation. | Segurola’s review synthesizes the coupled optical–rheological trade-off and cites Scheibler et al.’s 2024 copper study. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 3-4, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 4-5, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11) |
| Feedstock availability and alloy transferability | A powder qualified for MIM, LPBF, binder jetting, or extrusion is not automatically suitable for metal VPP: surface chemistry, oxide state, particle size, dispersion, optical response, and rheology all matter. Commercial feedstocks cover only a limited set of qualified alloys, and each powder–binder–printer–furnace combination needs validation. Incus literature documents successful 316L and copper processing, not universal metal compatibility. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 2-3, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 3-4, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 9-10, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloysa pages 9-11) |
| Cleaning and debinding | Surrounding uncured feedstock must be removed from surfaces and internal passages without eroding fragile green features. Blind, narrow, or tortuous channels may print successfully yet fail cleaning. During debinding, gas evolution and long transport paths can cause cracks, blisters, delamination, residue, or chemistry changes; the brown body may be weaker than the green body. | Incus processing involves decaking, solvent cleaning, solvent debinding, thermal debinding, and sintering; Segurola treats cleanability and geometry-specific debinding as separate qualification gates. (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 5-6, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 9-11, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys media 2245fb35) |
| Shrinkage and dimensional control | Shrinkage is anisotropic and geometry-, orientation-, packing-, furnace-load-, and setter-dependent. A single isotropic scale factor cannot reliably compensate walls, holes, lattices, and massive sections. Setters reduce sag but can constrain contraction, mark surfaces, or introduce contamination. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 7-8, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 9-10) |
| Reactive and precipitation-strengthened alloys | Alloys optimized for fusion AM may sinter poorly. For example, Cr₂Nb strengthens GRCop-42 but pins boundaries and inhibits pressureless densification; Cr/Nb oxides and trace water in hydrogen can impair wetting and disrupt phases. This is directly relevant to Cu–Cr–Zr, Cu–Cr–Nb, Al–Zr, and similar oxide-sensitive development programs. | Mastny’s GRCop-42 study found pressureless solid-state sintering impractical without additional liquid-phase strategies and documented oxide and wetting sensitivity. (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 5-9, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 11-14, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 14-17) |
| Qualification and standards | ISO/ASTM 52900 classifies the shaping step as vat photopolymerization, but the delivered product is a sintered metal part. Applicable frameworks include ISO/ASTM 52901, 52907, 52920, 52927, 52931, 52951, and 52953. These organize purchasing, powder characterization, site qualification, testing, safety, and data—not alloy-specific acceptance. MPIF Standard 35 remains a useful MIM/property comparator, but it does not qualify an LMM process or its dimensional capability. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 2-3, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 9-10, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11) |
| Competition from binder jetting | Binder jetting generally offers larger build envelopes, three-dimensional nesting, broader industrial powder ecosystems, and high green-part throughput. Its disadvantages are depowdering, lower green strength, binder-placement resolution, and the same furnace and shrinkage burden. Metal VPP competes where finer surfaces and smaller features justify lower scale and more difficult slurry handling. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9, EP3419802B1 pages 3-4, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 2-3, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 4-5) |
| Competition from micro-LPBF | Micro-LPBF directly consolidates metal and avoids cleaning uncured resin plus debinding, but carries melt-pool, support, residual-stress, reflectivity, thermal-distortion, powder-safety, and surface-roughness burdens. Metal VPP is attractive for reflective copper and fine, smooth batches, but only if sintering preserves chemistry, density, and dimensions. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 6-7, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 7-8, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 4-5) |
| Competition from MIM | MIM has mature feedstocks, furnaces, MPIF property data, high yield, and very low unit cost after mold tooling is amortized. Metal VPP removes hard tooling and supports rapid design changes, but retains most MIM downstream operations. Its economic window is therefore low-to-medium volume, high part variety, or geometry that is difficult to mold—not stable high-volume production. | (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 1-2, segurola2026…additivemanufacturingtechnology pages 5-7) |
| Key patent constraints | Relevant families include Steege/Trio Labs’ in-situ powder/resin infusion and projected-light powder-composite fabrication, priority 2016 and granted as EP3419802B1; Opschoor/ECN–Admatec’s metal-precursor slurry, conversion, debinding, and sintering route, priority 2015 and published as WO2017081160A1; and Caltech’s photopolymerized or infused metal-salt hydrogel routes. Claim scope, territorial status, ownership, and freedom to operate require patent-counsel review. | (EP3419802B1 pages 1-3, EP3419802B1 pages 3-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7, US20220314183A1 pages 71-74) |


*Table: Key technical, qualification, intellectual-property, and competitive barriers governing the commercial viability of sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization.*

**Standards and classification.** ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 classifies the shaping step as vat photopolymerisation, but the delivered material is sintered metal (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 2-3). Applicable standards include ISO/ASTM 52907 (powder characterisation), 52920 (production-site qualification), 52927 (main characteristics and test methods), 52931 (metallic-material safety), 52901 (purchased-part requirements), 52951 (data packages), and 52953 (process monitoring) (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 9-10, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 10-11). The NIST 2026 photopolymer workshop report identified unresolved measurement, data, safety, and standards gaps across photopolymer AM (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2). MPIF Standard 35 provides useful MIM-property comparator data but does not qualify an LMM process.

**Key patents.** The Steege/Trio Labs family (EP 3 419 802 B1, priority 2016) covers powder-composite fabrication using photocurable resin and particulate material with planar DLP or raster exposure, followed by debinding and sintering (EP3419802B1 pages 1-3, EP3419802B1 pages 3-4). The Opschoor/ECN–Admatec family (WO 2017 081 160 A1, priority 2015) covers metal-precursor-particle slurries with refractive-index matching to improve cure depth (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7). The Yee/Caltech family (US 2022/0314183 A1) covers photopolymerised or infused metal-salt hydrogel routes for metal-containing structures (US20220314183A1 pages 1-9, US20220314183A1 pages 71-74). Freedom-to-operate analysis requires patent-counsel review.

**Relevance to Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr alloys.** No peer-reviewed study demonstrating sinter-based VPP of aluminium alloys was found. Aluminium's tenacious oxide, high vapour pressure of alloying elements during sintering, and sensitivity to carbon/oxygen contamination from photopolymer binders present fundamental challenges that have not yet been addressed in the LMM literature. A lab with ultrasonic-atomised aluminium powder should expect substantial development work before LMM processing is feasible for these alloys.

## 5. Adjacent Routes

**Hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM).** Saccone et al. (2022, *Nature*) at Caltech (Greer group) demonstrated a VP-based route in which a DLP-printed PEGDA/DMF organogel scaffold is converted to a hydrogel, infused with aqueous metal-salt precursors, calcined to form metal oxide, and reduced to metal. The approach decouples geometry from composition: one photoresin supports many metals, including Cu, Ni, Ag, CuNi, the high-entropy alloy CuNiCoFe, refractory W-Ni, and Cu/Co multimaterials. Critical dimensions of ~40 μm and beam diameters below 50 μm were reported. The resulting metals exhibit highly twinned microstructures with annealing-twin densities of ~1.7 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ (Cu) and ~1.3 × 10⁶ m⁻¹ (CuNi), and nanoindentation hardness of 1.81 ± 0.37 GPa (Cu) and 2.15 ± 0.22 GPa (CuNi) (saccone2022additivemanufacturingof pages 1-2, saccone2022microscalefabricationof pages 1-4, saccone2022microscalefabricationof pages 6-9). HIAM remains a laboratory-scale method; commercialisation has not been reported.

**Metal-precursor photoresins.** The Opschoor/ECN patent approach substitutes metal-oxide or metal-salt precursor particles for metallic powder, exploiting the closer refractive-index match between precursors and resin to increase cure depth in highly loaded slurries. After photopolymerisation, an additional conversion step (hydrogen reduction, electro-deoxidation, or dehydride treatment) is required before sintering (WO2017081160A1 pages 1-4, WO2017081160A1 pages 4-7, WO2017081160A1 pages 15-17, WO2017081160A1 pages 23-25).

**Two-photon lithography (2PL) for metals.** Serles et al. (2026, *Nature Reviews Materials*) reviewed nanoscale AM of metals, alloys, and metal oxides, including 2PL with metallic nanoparticle-loaded resins and 2PL-HIAM, in which hydrogel templates are printed by two-photon lithography and infused with metal precursors. These approaches achieve sub-micrometre resolution but are presently limited to micro/nano-scale research structures (serles2026nanoscaleadditivemanufacturing pages 2-3).

## 6. Assessment and Outlook

Sinter-based metal VPP occupies a genuine but narrow commercial niche. Its mechanistic strengths—fine feature definition, smooth as-sintered surfaces, batch parallelism via whole-field exposure, compatibility with reflective and high-conductivity metals, and avoidance of melt-pool defects—are real but conditional on a fully qualified powder–binder–optical–thermal chain (segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 1-2, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 7-8, segurola2026lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 8-9). The commercial trajectory to date is cautionary: Holo's 2024 asset sale and Nano Dimension's 2025 exit from Admatec demonstrate that standalone metal-VPP ventures have struggled to reach self-sustaining scale. Incus remains the principal active printer vendor.

**Niches the process can hold:**
- **Copper thermal management** (cold plates, micro heat exchangers, electrical interconnects) where laser reflectivity limits LPBF and fine features exceed MIM mold capability.
- **Small, complex stainless-steel and titanium parts** in low-to-medium volumes where MIM tooling is uneconomic and binder jetting resolution is insufficient—orthodontic brackets, surgical instruments, watch components, micromechanical elements, RF waveguide features, and precision nozzles.
- **Precious metals** for jewelry and dental, where batch DLP of small parts is efficient and sintering infrastructure is established.
- **Shape-memory alloys (NiTi)** and specialty alloys for research and early-stage medical/aerospace prototyping, though carbon sensitivity demands careful binder chemistry.

**Where the process is unlikely to compete:**
- High-volume production (>~5,000–10,000 identical parts), where MIM's amortised tooling cost dominates.
- Large parts (typically >~50 mm), where binder jetting and LPBF offer vastly larger build envelopes.
- Alloys requiring very tight chemistry control (e.g., Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr) where binder-derived carbon and oxygen contamination is unacceptable and sintering science is immature.
- Precipitation-hardened copper alloys (Cu-Cr-Zr, GRCop-42) where pressureless sintering is fundamentally impeded by dispersoid-pinned grain boundaries and oxide sensitivity (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 5-9, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 11-14, mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 14-17).

**For a university alloy-development lab** with Al-Zr, Al-Mn-Cr-Zr, and Cu-Cr-Zr interests and its own ultrasonic atomisation capability, sinter-based metal VPP is currently most relevant as a copper and stainless-steel shaping route. Extending it to aluminium alloys or precipitation-strengthened copper alloys would require fundamental sintering research beyond the current state of the art. The lab's ultrasonic atomisation of fine powder (D50 < 20 μm) is well suited to the particle-size requirements of LMM feedstocks, but powder surface chemistry, oxide state, and compatibility with photocurable binders would need to be established experimentally for each alloy system.

## 1. Commercialization Landscape

Sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization (VPP) is an indirect additive-manufacturing route classified under ISO/ASTM 52900 as vat photopolymerisation. Patterned light selectively cures a photoactive binder loaded with metal powder layer by layer, producing a green composite that is subsequently cleaned, debound, and sintered—a process chain shared with metal injection molding (MIM) (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). **Incus GmbH** (Vienna, Austria, reported spinoff ~2019 from the Lithoz/TU Wien ecosystem) produces the Hammer Lab35 and Hammer Pro40 printers, which define "Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing" (LMM). The Hammer uses a top-exposure DLP projector above a cooled build platform; feedstock is a solid block of metal powder in a photocurable binder that is spread as a temperature-conditioned paste by a heated blade. The system has interchangeable small, medium, and large platform sizes. After printing, the green part is encased in surrounding feedstock, decaked, cleaned with the water-based solvent Incusol, solvent-debound, thermally debound, and sintered under reducing atmosphere (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000043). Incus has demonstrated 316L stainless steel and copper through to sintered components, and its promotional materials list 17-4PH, tool steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, and precious metals; peer-reviewed academic studies independently confirm 316L and Cu processing (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012). Installed base figures were not independently verified in the retrieved literature.

**Holo Inc.** (California, founded 2017; underlying patent priority 2016 from inventor Adam Steege at Trio Labs, Research Triangle Park, NC) developed the PureForm platform, a film-fed bottom-up DLP system for production of metal parts. The European patent EP 3 419 802 B1 (proprietor: Trio Labs, Inc.) covers a method and apparatus for solid freeform fabrication using particulate material combined with photocurable resin, planar DLP or raster exposure, debinding, and sintering (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000035). Holo reported pure copper parts exceeding 92% IACS conductivity, followed by 17-4PH and 316L stainless steels (vendor-reported figures). Holo's trajectory—from venture-backed startup to asset sale—constitutes a partial commercial failure of the standalone-printer business model, although the process survives as a contract service.

**Admatec Europe B.V.** (Alkmaar, Netherlands, reported founding ~2013) manufactures the Admaflex 130 and Admaflex 300 DLP printers, which use a tape-casting or slurry-delivery recoating mechanism (pqac-00000026). The company has a stronger commercial footprint in ceramic VPP (alumina, zirconia) than in metal VPP, though a related patent (WO 2017 081 160 A1, priority 2015, inventor Jan Opschoor, originally assigned to ECN) covers a radiation-curable slurry containing 55–98 wt% metal-precursor particles, photopolymerisation, debinding, precursor conversion, and sintering—an approach designed to improve optical penetration by using metal-oxide or metal-salt precursors whose refractive index better matches the resin (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041). **Nano Dimension acquired Admatec in 2022 and announced an exit/divestment in 2025**, a negative signal for standalone metal-DLP scale-up.

**Lithoz GmbH** (Vienna, founded 2011, TU Wien spinoff) is the parent-technology benchmark for lithography-based ceramic manufacturing (LCM) using CeraFab printers, from which Incus's metal-adapted technology emerged (pqac-00000012). Lithoz itself is not a principal metal-VPP supplier but its suspension-handling, debinding, and sintering knowledge base is foundational.

**3Dresyns / Resyner Technologies S.L.** (Donostia–San Sebastián, Spain) supplies open-material photopolymer binders, dispersants, and LMM feedstock formulations intended for user validation on SLA/DLP hardware, offering water- and solvent-debindable binder-route families (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000009).

## 2. Markets and Applications

Peer-reviewed evidence identifies several application domains, though independently verified production deployments at named end-users remain scarce.

**Copper thermal and electrical components.** Copper's high reflectivity makes it challenging for laser-based PBF, giving sinter-based VPP a mechanistic advantage. Scheibler et al. (2024) demonstrated LMM of copper on the Incus Hammer, characterising cure depth and green strength as functions of loading, particle size, and exposure (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). Roumanie et al. (2021) linked debinding and sintering conditions to copper composition and thermal conductivity in a highly loaded photocurable route (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). Target applications include micro heat exchangers, high-frequency components, cold plates, and electrical interconnects (pqac-00000012). Holo's copper-conductivity claims (>92% IACS) were directed at electronics thermal management, though these remain vendor-reported.

**Shape-memory and advanced alloys.** Cohen et al. (2023) demonstrated sinter-based LMM of NiTi shape-memory alloy and identified carbon/phase sensitivity in the process (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). This is relevant to medical devices and aerospace actuators, but the carbon sensitivity highlights that binder chemistry directly affects functional properties.

**Micro-architected metals and metamaterials.** Melentiev et al. (2024) demonstrated high-resolution 316L complex structures with fine features, hollow architectures, and measured surface/property data using DLP (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). The same group separately examined thin-walled 316L metamaterial debinding/sintering relationships (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009). These metamaterial and lattice demonstrations target lightweighting, energy absorption, and RF/microwave applications.

**Aerospace and GRCop alloys.** Mastny (2026) investigated pressureless liquid-phase sintering of GRCop-42 (Cu-4at.%Cr-2at.%Nb) for potential LMM processing, motivated by rocket-engine combustion-chamber applications. The study found that Cr₂Nb's grain-boundary pinning and oxide sensitivity made pressureless sintering impractical without liquid-phase aids (silver or bronze 90/10), and that trace water in hydrogen atmospheres degraded wettability (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). This result is directly relevant to a lab developing Cu-Cr-Zr complements: precipitation-strengthened copper alloys present fundamental sintering barriers that LMM inherits.

**Watch, jewelry, dental, and micromechanics.** Incus lists precious metals and watch/jewelry components among its application targets (vendor-reported). The parent ceramic-VPP ecosystem (Lithoz) has well-documented dental applications. Metal VPP's fine surface finish and batch capability are suited to orthodontic brackets, watch cases, and small medical instruments, though named commercial deployments were not independently verified in the retrieved literature.

## 3. Economics

Quantitative economic data for metal VPP is largely vendor-proprietary. Segurola (2026) provides the most rigorous framework, defining complete-cell economics rather than printer-level metrics (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032):

- **Effective cell throughput** = accepted components delivered / complete elapsed factory-cell time, measured at steady state.
- **Material efficiency** = mass of accepted parts / mass of released input.
- **Cost per accepted part** includes equipment amortisation, occupancy, consumables (feedstock, solvents, setters, gas), labour, queue time, yield loss, failed qualification, and scrap.

The review explicitly states that "printer capital cost is not complete-cell cost" and that the route requires optical calibration, cleaning equipment, ventilation, solvent/water management, debinding and sintering furnaces, gas supply, setters, metrology, maintenance, and qualified personnel (pqac-00000007). Whole-field DLP exposure can reduce dependence of exposure time on part count within one image, but nesting, cross-sectional area, layer renewal, separation, cleaning, and furnace capacity still govern throughput. A full plate of thin parts may expose efficiently and overload cleaning or furnace fixturing (pqac-00000007).

The technology selection framework (ER-139) further notes that comparisons must freeze annual volume, part mix, geometry, acceptance criteria, and comparator; AM should not receive credit for unused geometric freedom, and MIM or machining comparators should not be burdened with tooling assumptions absent from the actual case (pqac-00000032).

**Indicative positioning versus competitors** (largely from vendor and trade sources, flagged accordingly):
- *Versus MIM:* Metal VPP eliminates mold tooling (typically $10 k–$100 k+) and supports rapid design iteration, but retains all downstream MIM operations (debinding, sintering, inspection). The break-even volume against MIM is therefore low—typically cited by vendors as hundreds to low thousands of parts, below which mold amortisation makes MIM uneconomic.
- *Versus binder jetting:* Binder jetting offers larger build envelopes, 3D nesting, broader powder ecosystems, and higher green throughput, but with coarser resolution and depowdering requirements. Metal VPP competes where finer surfaces and smaller features justify smaller scale and more difficult feedstock handling (pqac-00000031).
- *Versus micro-LPBF:* Micro-LPBF directly consolidates metal, avoiding debinding, but carries melt-pool, support, residual-stress, reflectivity, and surface-roughness burdens. Metal VPP is attractive for reflective metals (copper) and for fine, smooth batch production (pqac-00000031).

**Printer pricing** is not published in the peer-reviewed literature. Vendor-reported figures place the Incus Hammer systems in the range typical of industrial ceramic/metal DLP systems (roughly €200 k–€500 k, vendor data); Admaflex 130 systems are reported at a lower entry point. These figures exclude furnaces, cleaning stations, and ancillary infrastructure.
